subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENTS PROVIDING FOR CO-OPERATION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENTS PROVIDING FOR CO-OPERATION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs has asked me to table copies in English and in French of the following agreements: Agreement for co-operation concerning civil uses of atomic energy between the government of the United States and the government of Canada; agreement between the government of the United States of America and the government of Canada for co-operation regarding atomic information for mutual defence purposes.
These agreements were signed in Washington on June 15, 1955, and are the ones to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred in his announcement to the house on that date. The Minister of Trade and Commerce intends in a few moments to make an explanatory statement on the agreement concerning civil uses of atomic energy and the Minister of National Defence on the agreement regarding atomic information for mutual defence purposes on another occasion.
Copies of these agreements will be available in the joint parliamentary distribution branch.

maintopic: STATEMENT CONCERNING AGREEMENT ON CIVIL USES OF ATOMIC ENERGY

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, as the agreement concerning the civil uses of atomic energy which has just been tabled is a somewhat lengthy and technical document, I think it may be helpful if I draw to the attention of the house its main features and their significance to Canada. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said last Wednesday when he announced that the agreement had been signed, the agreement has been made possible by the revision of the United States Atomic Energy Act in 1954. This agreement has been prepared in order to take advantage of the extension of the areas of co-operation made possible by the new United States act. This act now provides
for an exchange of information and other forms of co-operation in the following fields:
(1)	Refining, purification, and subsequent treatment of source material.
(2)	Reactor development.
(3)	Production of special nuclear material.
(4)	Health and safety.
(5)	Industrial and other applications of atomic energy for peaceful purposes.
(6)	Research and development relating to the foregoing.
The agreement which has just been executed is designed to take advantage of this fact. The preamble to the agreement records briefly the collaboration which has taken place between Canada and the United States since the inception of the atomic energy program in the war years, and establishes a general basis for future co-operation. The body of the agreement specifies the manner in which co-operation in the six areas I have just mentioned will take place.
The agreement, of course, confers advantages on both countries. From Canada's standpoint it will be of particular value that we will now have access to information on the several types of demonstration power reactors which are being built in the United States. This information will be most helpful in comparing the performances of the different types of demonstration reactors now under design and construction in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. Another important benefit to the agreement is that it also provides for a more complete exchange of information in the purely scenti-fic field, which, of course, is fundamental to our progress in the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. While the purpose of the agreement is to further the civil application of atomic energy, it must be recognized that much of the information which will be exchanged also has military significance. Consequently, the agreement contains certain provisions relating to the safeguarding of such information.
The agreement marks a further stage in Canada's close collaboration with the United States in the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes.

subtopic: MURIEL CLAIRE WILSON HART

speechtext:
On the order:
An act to repeal an act of the present session intituled: "An act for the relief of Muriel Claire Wilson Hart".-Mr. Regier.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MURIEL CLAIRE WILSON HART
subsubtopic: BILL TO REPEAL ACT RULED OUT OF ORDER
speechtext:
It will come as no surprise to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam if I tell him and the house that I have received from the law clerk an opinion in which he says:
The introduction of this bill should be ruled out of order for two principal reasons: First, it is a public bill to repeal a private act; and, second, it is absolutely of no effect.
As to the first point, the divorce act which Mr. Regier's bill is intended to repeal is a private act passed at the request and in the interest of only one person. This divorce act was carefully studied in the Senate divorce committee, which rendered its decision only after very serious consideration; it then passed through the various stages in the Senate and the House of Commons, and received royal assent without opposition. Even if this act could be affected by legislation, it would have to be done by private legislation as by no stretch of the imagination can this matter be deemed to have attained such proportions as would justify a public bill in the public interest. The decision of parliament has been, to use Mr. Regier's expression, that of the highest court in the land. In a divorce case, more particularly, it can be said that this is a decision of a court. Under parliamentary practice, parliament, except in a very extreme case of great public interest, could not by public act set aside a decision of a court that it has itself set up, whose procedure it has devised, and which is under its direct control. Until parliament decides that divorces shall be granted by public acts, because each case is a matter of general interest, annulling a divorce, if it could be done, should be accomplished by private legislation.
As to the second point, an act for the repeal of a divorce act is of absolutely no effect. Section 15 of the Interpretation Act states that every act shall be deemed remedial. Is this act remedial? Let us look at section 19, which, in part, states:
19. (1) Where any act or enactment is repealed, or where any regulation is revoked, then, unless the contrary intention appears, such repeal or revocation does not, save as in this section otherwise provided,
(b)	affect the previous operation of any act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked, or anything duly done or suffered thereunder,
(c)	affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred under the act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked.
If we ask ourselves what was the previous operation of this divorce act duly assented to, it was,
as stated in the act, that:
1.	The said marriage between Muriel Claire Wilson and Lawrence Hart, her husband, is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
2.	The said Muriel Claire Wilson may at any time hereafter marry any man whom she might lawfully marry if the said marriage with the said Lawrence Hart had not been solemnized. The result is that the tie which united Muriel
Claire Wilson and Lawrence Hart, her husband,

Questions
has been broken, and the fact of repealing the act which did this would not have the effect of marrying them a second time. One might even ask: "Supposing one of the parties has married again since the divorce was granted, would an act repealing this divorce render that party guilty of bigamy?"
Once parliament has completely dissolved a marriage, it can no more adopt legislation to say that the said marriage has not been dissolved than it could, if a rope has been cut, affirm in its legislation that this rope has not been cut.
Therefore, I submit the proposed bill is out of order as it is contrary to the rules which make the distinctions between public and private bills; and it is frivolous since it can have no possible effect.
Respectfully submitted,
Maurice Ollivier,
Law Clerk,
House of Commons.
In view of this opinion, I declare the introduction of this bill out of order.

speechtext:
1.	How many derailments were there on the Edmundston division of the Canadian National Railways between November 1, 1954 and May 1, 1955?
2.	What was the total cost to the railway of such derailments?
3.	How many regular section men were laid off on the Edmundston division between November 1, 1954 and May 1, 1955?

subtopic: C.N.R. EDMUNDSTON DIVISION   DERAILMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1.	Fifteen. Heavy traffic on this division during the war years greatly burdened the track structure. A major program of rehabilitation was begun two years ago, and it is expected that the greater portion of the work will have been completed by the end of the
present year. The total expenditures for such work will have amounted to approximately $4 million.
2.	The repair work to track and equipment was performed by company forces and the costs of such repairs are assembled under various categories in the company's operating expense accounts. In accordance with normal railway accounting practice, these costs are not itemized with respect to specific derailments. Certain of the costs are specifically identifiable, notably the cost of clearing and repairing track and claims in respect of injuries and damage to freight. The aggregate of these costs was $148,339.75. The cost of equipment destroyed and retired was $92,753. This amount is chargeable against the depreciation reserve which is accrued on a mortality basis which takes cognizance of retirements occasioned by accidents. The costs for repairs to other equipment includes unascertained portions attributable to accidents and to normal program maintenance carried out while the equipment was in the shops.
3.	None.
4.	The sections range from eight to thirteen miles in length, the average being 9-67 miles. The number of men per section ranges from three to four, the average being 3-24 men.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I was absent in Alberta last week, the hon. Leader of the Opposition asked the following question, and I quote from page 4813 of Hansard:
In the absence of the Minister of Justice, Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that the Conrad Hilton chain is now operating under a contract with the publicly owned hotel which is in process of construction in Montreal-in the absence of the minister the Prime Minister may prefer to take this as notice-has consideration been given to the effect under the Combines Investigation Act of the agreement made between the Canadian National Railways and the Conrad Hilton chain from the point of view of the restrictive practices outlined in that agreement?
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the answer to the hon. gentleman's question is as follows. The combines branch has noted the reports about a management contract between the Canadian National Railways and the Hilton hotel group. Since the information before the branch does not indicate that the Hilton group has other hotel interests in Canada, any such contract would not appear to give rise to inquiry under the Combines Investigation Act.

Inquiries of the Ministry In other words, in so far as Canada is concerned this would seem to be a case of substituting one independent management for another, rather than a combination or merger between two groups already in the country.
There is also doubt that hotel accommodation could be considered an article or commodity, within the meaning of the anticombines legislation, which refers to combinations and mergers in respect of articles and commodities.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, June 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe, Port Arthur (for Mr. St. Laurent) for the second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I continue this debate today with a good deal of encouragement. As I pointed out during the time when this subject was under discussion, the problems of parliament demand vigilance not only from parliament itself but from the press and from the public generally. That is, in fact, the very essence of a vigorous and vital democracy.
At first, as we must all recognize, little interest in this measure now before us was shown by the press generally. So far as many of the newspapers were concerned, this was simply another piece of legislation. Now the press and the public are showing interest and I trust that the government-and above all the members opposite who will be responsible if this bill passes-are showing an interest in what the press is saying. If we believe in the value of a free press we must also, I think, attach some importance to a general sentiment that is being expressed with regard to the legislation we are asked to consider. In addition to that letters to the press, which express public opinion and are in themselves a reflection of public opinion, show growing concern with regard to the extension of these wide-open powers without any limit as to time or other restriction.
I recognize the rule against quoting editorials which would reflect upon the government, and I do not intend to do so; but under the rules I am permitted to summarize the effect of those editorials and it is uniformly-with only two or three exceptions- one of condemnation of the attempt to make these wide and arbitrary powers a permanent part of our legislation. There were two very understandable exceptions. One was the Montreal Star and the other the Winnipeg Free Press. I mention these because they are very responsible newspapers with a substantial circulation which naturally affects the general thinking of many people. If I have omitted any others which have shown a lack of interest in the dangers inherent in this measure, then I apologize because that would be simply based upon the fact that they have not been drawn to my attention.
May I point out that even these editorials indicate the need for extended debate. At 50433-315J
Defence Production Act first it was obvious there was little understanding of the dangers inherent in what we are asked to do. Then, as the measure was examined and the effect of an extension of these powers was better understood, a vigilant press and a vigilant public began to indicate their opinion. Nevertheless, the need for further discussion and further emphasis is placed before us clearly by the editorials to which I have referred. In the case of the Montreal Star, they refer to the need for continuing the emergency powers act. They point out that it may well be accepted as the minimum that is required. It says, without quoting the exact words, that without the emergency powers act the government would be forced to invoke the War Measures Act.
It is necessary for me, Mr. Speaker, to point out to the Montreal Star that the emergency powers act was repealed last year. At that time when the ordinary consideration of that bill was before the house the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) clearly indicated that while there was still some reason for concern the situation had reached a point where it was not necessary to continue the emergency powers act. We are not being asked to consider that. We are being asked to consider an act which does not declare an emergency but merely tries to write into our permanent law wide powers which would have the effect of actually cutting right across the powers of parliament and the rights of provincial governments in relation to property and civil rights.
I would refer to the editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press. On some occasions I have not agreed entirely with the Winnipeg Free Press, but on this occasion I must say that this is one of the most amusing editorials that newspaper has produced. It points out that it is silly of the Minister of Defence Production to introduce this bill. Those are the words of the Winnipeg Free Press, not mine. It points out that he has offered no reason for a continuation of these wide powers. Then, of course, just so that everything will be balanced fairly, it says that the opposition is silly in its insistence upon the position we take. It points out we are silly because we do not understand the motives of the government. Well, Mr. Speaker, I concede right away that we do not understand the motives of the government. Ever since the resolution was introduced in March which declared that it was expedient that such a bill be introduced, we have been trying to understand the motives of the government in introducing this measure this year. The Defence Production Act will still be on the statute books untouched in any way, unlimited in its powers and fully effective until July 31, 1956. We

Defence Production Act certainly do not understand the motives of the government in introducing this measure. So that everything will be fair all round, may I say that I think this is the silliest editorial I have ever read. It does not even attempt to understand what the issue is.
Oh, how I wish that some of the Liberals who have read this editorial would look back to the liberalism of the Manchester Guardian. What a wonderful thing it would be if in the Winnipeg Free Press we heard the authentic voice of liberalism such as is expressed on the pages of the Manchester Guardian. I mention that because the Winnipeg Free Press does purport to express the true brand of undiluted liberalism.

No, Mr. Speaker, the liberalism that is being put forward in this act is not liberalism nor is it progressive. This is a reversion to something that has not happened since the days of the Tudors and the Stuarts. This is an attempt to take away from parliament the authority of parliament over the whole economy, except to such extent as the government sees fit to leave this in our hands.
The Winnipeg Free Press does go on to give some practical advice. Perhaps this comes closer to the voice of the Manchester Guardian. It says that while it is silly for the Minister of Defence Production to want these powers, nevertheless it will not be so bad if the other members of the government will only exercise some supervision over this minister who is making a silly demand. It is important that we realize that the government is not able to exercise supervision; that this measure not only takes away the authority of parliament but it also takes away the authority of the government in most cases, and that it leaves to the pure, untrammelled discretion of the minister himself, the decision as to how far we shall remain as a parliament.
Actually, when the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) spoke about the true sentiments of liberalism, I could not help recalling the occasion when people were not vigilant, and they saw their rights disappear under the most earnest demands and under the most intense religious appeal. I think, as a matter of fact, there is a speech that would be worth rereading by a number of hon. members opposite, and I am placing this argument forward in all earnestness. This was a speech made exactly 300 years ago. I know that there are those who say, oh, do not bother about these old, dusty arguments out of the distant past. But let us remember that in January of 1655 Oliver Cromwell made a very important speech in


the House of Commons in Britain. He was urging wide powers that were not restrained by parliament, and he put forward the same idea that the people should trust him. Then, he used these significant words:
And the people being the blessing of God, they will not be so angry but they will prefer their safety to their passions, and their real security to forms . . .
The protector, as he described himself, but the dictator as he became known in history, in the name of God decided that it was in the interests of the people that they should not bother about forms like the mace, which he called a bauble, and decided they should have the kind of security that comes from arbitrary power. And so having decided that in the name of God it was wise that he should no longer be disturbed by that nuisance of parliament, he then closed that very famous speech with these words:
I think it my duty to tell you that it is not for the profit of these nations nor for common and public good for you to continue here any longer. And therefore I do declare unto you that I do dissolve this parliament.
Now, it may not be in the minds of any hon. members to go that far. But the fact is that the measure before us, which we are asked to embed, for all practical purposes, in the permanent laws of Canada, places it in the hands of the government to say exactly what Cromwell said 300 years ago last January.
Now, I still hope that hon. members opposite will examine this carefully, and that both the government and the members supporting it will take the advice of the Winnipeg Free Press in this instance. I know that many of them pay a great deal of attention to the Winnipeg Free Press, whether it is speaking the authentic voice of Canadian liberalism or the Manchester Guardian brand. But the fact remains that I wish they would pay attention to the need for supervision of the actions of any minister, and that they would therefore examine this act carefully and see just how far it goes. I hope that, with the change that has taken place in the thinking across this country, many hon. members will reread this act carefully. This act would be continued indefinitely by the amendments now before us. And, Mr. Speaker, in a world in which hope still springs eternal, I wonder if it is too much to hope that the Minister of Defence Production may actually have some little doubt about his own infallibility. That would be a wonderful and encouraging sign, that this debate and discussion have produced some results, results which we are seeing have some impact outside the house.

I have already pointed out what editorials are saying, one in a very responsible newspaper in eastern Canada which thinks we are discussing the Emergency Powers Act, and the other which agrees that the minister is silly in demanding these powers but thinks that the opposition is silly in criticizing the continuation of those powers.
For that reason every hon. member should realize how uncertain the government's position is. And obviously of course the minister is uncertain-and as he is leaving the chamber now I must direct my remarks to hon. members opposite, because it is their vote that is of importance and their decision that is of importance. Because we have seen so far-and I am glad to see the minister is now returning-

I am glad to have the minister back with us, because we are always hopeful that as a result of a vigilant press, a vigilant public, and a vigilant House of Commons, the minister may decide that he is not infallible, and may decide that an act for which he was responsible, and for the drafting of which he has told us he was mainly responsible, may be reviewed and revised.
There is one thing about the Minister of Defence Production, and that is that he always provides an interjection that is worth looking back to. The other day he said that it was drafted by a Tory. It is interesting to have the Minister of Defence Production describing himself as a Tory. I do not understand that remark. He added that, at the request of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) he was responsible for the group which drafted this act, and then on another occasion he said that he drafted it.
There is of course no argument that has been made by the minister or by any member of the government, or indeed by anyone on the other side of the house, which has told us why this bill we now have before us that gives powers to the minister indefinitely, which gives powers that will continue permanently on the statute books, should be continued beyond July 31 next-that is, unless we are not going to be permitted to meet before that.
There is one argument however that is clear, and that is the argument put forward by the socialists. They do not leave any doubt as to what they think this act should mean. They have made it clear that they think this act is an attack on capitalism.
Defence Production Act They think this is an act which should be used as a club over the heads of private enterprise.
Well, I am just waiting for a single member of the government to repudiate the explanation given by the socialists for their support of this act. In this case I agree with their argument, although I do not agree with the decision they make as to how they will vote. I can understand their vote. They believe in putting socialism into effect, without even having to consult parliament-and under the terms of this very act we are now discussing they can do so.
The government has not said, "We repudiate completely the explanation given by our socialist supporters. That is not the reason this act is before us". We are still waiting to be told why it is that they want to make this a permanent part of our laws.
Now, we should have not only an explanation from some member of the government, but we should have an explanation from the Prime Minister. I know of course that the Prime Minister is at the moment engaged in a conference. However, I am perfectly certain that the discussion here will be drawn to his attention; and as this debate will not be terminated for some time there will be opportunity for him to consider what is being said. I hope the Prime Minister will recognize that he should speak in this debate.
We have been told that this act is more restrictive than that in the United Kingdom or in the United States. Even the most cursory examination of the act will show just how remote from reality is that statement by the Minister of Defence Production. The Prime Minister is a lawyer, and as head of the government he is the individual entrusted by the Queen's representative for the responsibility of government; and he should clear away that misapprehension which is in the minds of hon. members.
There is another misapprehension in the minds of hon. members opposite, one which has been indicated in the speeches of those who have spoken. The principle at issue in the measure now before us is not that of the setting up of the Department of Defence Production. The bill now before us, as was pointed out by the minister-and it seems to have been forgotten by many hon. members-is a bill containing only two clauses. The first clause simply changes the salary of the minister from $10,000 to $15,000. That is merely a formal change, to make the payment of salary to the minister coincide with the salaries of ministers in other departments. There is no question of principle involved there. It is merely a formal adjustment.

Defence Production Act It is the second clause that raises the whole principle, and the only principle, before us in this debate. Clause 2 is the clause we must examine. It is a very short one stating that "section 41 of the said act is repealed".
That means only one thing, and it raises the whole principle we are discussing. This clause, if accepted, would strike out section 41 in the act, which reads as follows:
This act, except subsection (6) of section 4, shall expire on the 31st day of July, 1956.
Therefore, the principle involved is whether or not we shall embed in the permanent laws of Canada all these wide powers that were placed before us in 1951 when there was so much uncertainty in the mind of everyone at the time of the very severe war in Korea.
It will be recalled that on that occasion we had suddenly been forced to change our whole course. We had been giving up many of the military machines and weapons accumulated after the war. We had, in fact, been advancing into what we thought was a period of increasing peace. Then suddenly war, and bloody war, broke out in Korea in June of 1950. Then we were called upon to reverse our whole trend; we were called upon to change our thinking about defence. Suddenly we were called upon to improvise once again, as we have been called upon to do on other occasions. A hastily drafted bill was placed before us. At that time we made it abundantly clear that we thought the bill was badly drawn, and why would it not be badly drawn when it was drawn by the Minister of Defence Production? I say that simply because we know his attitude toward parliament. He has told us he thinks that some people think it is a good thing to have a forum for discussion, but he does not like that. He does not like parliament, and leaves no doubt about it.
He drafted the bill with the idea that he would not have to bother too much about parliament. We pointed out the dangers. They are on records Hansard shows exactly what we said at that time. We left no uncertainty. When any hon. member on the other side suggests that we are opposing simply for the sake of opposing, I suggest that they look back to what was said in 1951 when this hastily drafted bill was before us. We made it clear then that we wanted a Department of Defence Production, and we made it clear that we were not going to oppose the actual implementation of the request for a Department of Defence Production, and that we were not going to vote against the bill, and we did not because there was a definite time limit.
To that extent we took the assurance of the government that this bill contained powers that they would not continue. That was their statement; that was the assurance upon which I assumed-and I certainly have the right to assume-that hon. members opposite voted in support of this measure. We did not oppose the adoption of the measure at that time because the government had insisted that this was only a temporary measure. I made our position clear. I will briefly refer to what I said on March 2, 1951, as reported at page 847 of Hansard:
In so far as the bill sets up a department of defence production and gives proper authority to carry out the appropriate duties of that department, I feel sure there is approval throughout the whole of the house.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what possibly could be clearer that that-approval throughout the whole of this house of the setting up of a department of defence production? That is not an issue before us. Nothing that is before us has anything to do with the continuance of the Department of Defence Production.
We pointed out, however, that while agreeing to the Department of Defence Production, we believed that at a time when we were fighting for democracy the very foundation of democracy should be preserved here in this parliament. We urged that there be a recognition that the measures in this act challenged the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law upon which our whole theory of parliamentary democracy rests.
When the motion came before the house three months ago that it was expedient to introduce the measure now before us, we urged the government to redraft the bill so that the Department of Defence Production
would operate under clearly defined powers. This is what I said on March 14 of this year, as reported at page 1987 of Hansard:
I would hope that the Prime Minister would seize this opportunity to carry out the statement which was made on behalf of the government in 1951 to the effect that some of the powers in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature, and to find how best the nowers that are needed can be defined and described without leaving the wide, unlimited powers which have existed over these past few years. It is not enough to say that these powers have not been employed. The very fact that these powers might be used to persuade somebody to do something without the actual formal exercise of those powers, is in itself a sufficient exercise of those nowers to put us on our guard at this time.
Other members in the house argued that the original bill should be redrafted, and that in any event it should not be renewed without some time limit. We had reason to believe that the government had listened to those arguments and was going to act upon them. Before the debate was closed that day and

the motion was adopted the Prime Minister assured the house that the government would give consideration to the views that had been expressed.
Since the Prime Minister gave the assurance that consideration would be given, surely he owes it to the house to say what the decision was and why, after due consideration, with three months to do it, no attempt has been made to redraft this bill.
Some hon. members opposite dismiss the whole discussion as though it were a discussion that had no relation to the problems before us. If that is so, why did the Prime Minister assure the house on March 14 that consideration would be given to these discussions? We want to know from him exactly why it is that this bill is now before us to perpetuate those powers without any restriction to the extent of their application.
The strongest argument against the adoption of this bill comes from the government itself, Mr. Speaker. Again it seems necessary to repeat. When this bill was before us in the first instance in 1951 the government emphasized that they would not ask the house to make this permanent law because it contained powers that should not be continued. Their argument is the strongest argument why this amendment should not be adopted by this house.
If that assurance means nothing, if the assurance on which hon. members permitted this bill to pass in 1951 means nothing, if those words are to be completely disregarded, how can any assurance which the government now gives have the slightest value at this time? If their assurance then constituted nothing upon which we were to rely, then how can we rely upon any statement now as to what they propose to do? I submit, Mr. Speaker, there are several reasons why the government should not proceed with this bill. I am making these arguments now in all seriousness to the government, to hon. members opposite and also in the hope that it may correct some of the misapprehensions which obviously still exist outside of this house. These are the particular reasons why it seems now that the government should not proceed with this bill.
First, it does not need to be dealt with in any event at this session. The present act continues, as I have pointed out already, until July 31, 1956. Surely it would be much better to wait until next session and in the light of conditions as they are at that time to place before this house an appropriate measure carefully drafted by legal draftsmen in keeping with conditions as they actually are.
Defence Production Act
The second reason why this bill should not be passed is that the act was adopted on the assurance that the government recognized that these powers should not be continued.
Third, it should not be passed because no time limit is placed on the duration of the legislation.
Fourth, the act as it stands is a denial of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.
Fifth, the only legislation necessary is legislation continuing the Department of Defence Production. If the Department of Defence Production is continued and these loose and indefinite powers are omitted, then automatically the government can bring into effect a statute already on the statute books, the Defence Supplies Act, which is similar to the act in the United Kingdom to which reference was made by the Minister of Defence Production when he drew an incorrect interpretation that it was as wide in its powers as this act.
I urge upon hon. members opposite to pay attention to the things that are being said outside this house. After all, why do we support the principle of a free press? We support the principle of a free press because a free press is expected and I think has the duty to interpret public sentiment and to indicate what it believes the public wants and demands. Surely no one reading the editorial comment across Canada today can be in any doubt that the majority of the newspapers in Canada have come to the conclusion that the powers in the Defence Production Act should not be embodied in the permanent laws of this country.
An ingenious argument was put forward on the other side of the house. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) made an extraordinarily interesting argument when he argued in effect that a lot of this bill was ultra vires anyway. He argued that if some of these powers were exercised the courts would not permit them to be exercised. In case hon. members opposite are being beguiled by that argument and have any idea that the courts will protect them against the effect of this act because no emergency is declared in the act, I suggest that they should go back and examine the legal history of legislation of a similar nature.
If the court concludes that there was an emergency and that it can be understood from the discussion which took place at the time the act was being put into effect; if hon. members think that the courts will declare that the act comes under the general provisions of peace, order and good government, then I suggest that the hon. member

Defence Production Act for Rosthern and any hon. members who may have taken to heart the argument he made as perhaps salving their consciences to some extent in supporting legislation of this kind should examine a case which was decided in 1946 by the privy council.
I understand that it is not yet an offence to recite judgments of the privy council in view of the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) still carries cases there although he has indicated that he does not think it is in keeping with our sovereignty to do so. He still goes back there, and then having gone back there he does not pay much attention to the judgment which he gets, as was the case last year.
There was a case decided in 1946 by the privy council and the judgment is to be found at page 193 of Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1946. That case involved the attorney general for Ontario and others, appellants, and Canada Temperance Federation and others, respondents. I am not going to go into the details of that case except to say that it had to do with the Canada Temperance Act which was enacted many years ago by the parliament of Canada. All hon. members will realize that in the ordinary course of events the supervision of the disposition of spirits and the supervision of the conduct of those who have absorbed spirits come under provincial administration.
The parliament of Canada passed the Canada Temperance Act in 1878 and that statute, amended or replaced by subsequent amendments, is still on the statute books of Canada. Rightly or wrongly, certain provincial governments thought that it would simplify the administration of their liquor legislation and the control of the results of the sale of liquor if there was not conflict between the Canada Temperance Act and the provincial acts dealing with the same subject. This particular case was fought out in the courts and carried to the privy council which decided that although there was no declaration of an emergency in the Canada Temperance Act, having regard to what was said at the time and the nature of the act that was introduced, the court must assume that there had been something in the nature of an emergency in Canada in 1878 in regard to the consumption of spirituous liquors. That is an interesting bit of ancient history, but nevertheless the court decided that the government of Canada felt that there was an emergency with which they must deal and therefore they passed an act to deal with something that would ordinarily be under provincial jurisdiction without any question. They held that they were bound to take the position that the members of parliament

of that time must have dealt with the act in the belief that an emergency actually existed.
That is on all fours with the present case. Although there is no emergency declared by the statute,, this act was introduced with statements that indicated the belief that there was an emergency. We have had the statement of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) that there is an emergency and that the situation is more critical than it was in 1951 when the Defence Production Act was originally passed. Of course at that point it does seem to become necessary to recall that although the Minister of Defence Production had that opinion the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) did not share the same opinion. Just four days ago the Minister of National Defence, on more than one occasion in his speech, on at least three occasions, clearly stated that there appeared to be a lessening of the tension in the cold war. In fact, he used the rather appealing words toward the end of his speech that the present climate of international affairs appeared to be moderating. Last year, before the minister of national defence at that time was prepared to make any such statement, the government permitted the Emergency Powers Act to lapse. Now the Minister of Defence Production says that the emergency is greater than in 1951. If, at some time 40 or 50 years from now, a court were called upon to interpret this act, they could not overlook the statement of the Minister of Defence Production that this act was being put forward with that thought in mind. Just as the privy council decided, in the case to which I have already referred, in 1946, that there must have been an emergency in the minds of the members of parliament, a court at some distant date in the future would be bound to hold the same opinion and would say that the Minister of Defence Production, who had most to say about this act on behalf of the government, regarded the emergency as greater than it had been in the early stages of the very severe war in Korea.

Mr. Speaker, the minister does not understand the meaning of statute, nor apparently the meaning of his own words. The law is there. What he is asking us to do is not to exercise the powers that were put on the books until July 31, 1956. He is asking us to continue indefinitely into the future powers which he said on March 11 should not be continuing powers. That is his statement. No, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Defence Production cannot even remember the effect of what he says. Yet he asks you to support him in the continuation indefinitely of powers which he said should not be indefinite.
Now, this act, of course, is an act that is part of a general trend which all hon. members should recognize. The hon. members opposite should not take so much to heart the contention that it is a time for us to reverse our course. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) did some fantastic special pleading the other day. He said that what we have before us is the question of whether we are going to have defence production or not. Well, there is not a parliamentary word that describes that statement of the senior member for Halifax. There is not a word that would be permitted by the Speaker within the rules of parliament that would adequately describe in its fantastic nonsense the statement by the hon. member that the issue before us is whether we are going to have defence production. Where in the bill before us is there any suggestion of that kind? Where in those two sections is that to be found? On the contrary, he has on Hansard, as every other hon. member has, the unreserved statement that all of us-every hon. member-want a Department of Defence Production. He has the fact that we supported that, when that was in fact the principle, as we pointed out. That is not the principle now. The only principle before the members is whether or not this parliament is going to submit meekly to the demand of the Minister of Defence Production, "With me it is all or nothing".

Defence Production Act Mr. Drew: Yes, I said that before, and obviously the hon. member needs to have it repeated, as some hon. members do, because that is the only argument that has been made. The hon. Minister of Defence Production is demanding his pound of flesh. He has not been happy about the way things have gone. With him it is all or nothing. Well, I should like to think what would have been said by some hon. members of the Liberal party of earlier days if they had been told this-and it is they who are being told, because it is their vote that is going to put this into effect along with the socialist vote, if it goes into effect. They are the ones who should be the most critical, and I should like to think of some great Liberals of other days sitting quietly in their seats and being told, "I don't care what any other hon. member thinks; with me it is all or nothing". That is the actual effect of this measure, and that is exactly what the minister has said. He wants the whole hog or nothing. I hope the hon. members opposite will realize that the principle involved is the writing into our permanent laws in perpetuity of an act that by-passes parliament, and in a substantial measure by-passes even the supervision of government itself. This problem of delegated powers is not one unique here, and the hon. members opposite should not be sensitive about discussion of this subject, because this is a subject which applies to all parties and in all countries where there is parliamentary democracy.
Under the demands of war, starting with the first world war, it became necessary under the immense pressures created to adopt measures which were not consistent with our parliamentary traditions. However, every hon. member who did recall the great traditions of parliament made it clear that we should drop those powers and powers of that kind just as soon as an orderly way of life-no matter what the pressures might be-made it possible to return to true parliamentary democracy.
The same thing has happened in Britain. The same thing has happened in Australia, in New Zealand and elsewhere. The subject has been discussed. In Britain a strong committee was set up to examine this question of delegated powers. This government does not like setting up committees that really have the power to act. It prefers a committee where the guillotine can be employed at the appropriate time. Unfortunately, the real effectiveness of committees has not been recognized. When a government bill is brought before parliament in a form which, even in regard to merely executive or administrative matters, gives a wide or unlimited discretion to a minister, and objection is made, the answer is sometimes given that the minister may be trusted by the house to use his powers with a wise and reasonable discretion. The answer may be perfectly bona fide: but temvora mutanturt and another minister or another government may use the unlimited powers indiscreetly or oppressively.
It is obvious that in the United Kingdom, as here, no matter what the law is, there are those who are prepared to say, "We trust the minister". Lord Justice Scott was pointing out that it is not enough to trust any minister but that our parliamentary system demands that we examine what any minister at any time can do under measures passed by parliament and that when there is delegated authority we should be particularly careful to remember the ancient legal doctrine delegata potestas non potest delegari. The ancient legal maxim that a person to whom powers have been delegated cannot delegate them to others rests upon the clear idea that if someone delegates power to a particular individual, then it should not be permitted for that individual to delegate them to some other person, a person wholly unknown to the person who has delegated the original powers.
This act flies right in the face of the ancient legal maxim. It delegates power and it permits the minister to delegate power and it writes into the law in perpetuity the delegation of those powers. The very fact that we now, in June of 1955, are called upon to make permanent an act which will not come to an end until July 31, 1956, is the best possible evidence that this government intends to make these powers permanent.
I want to point out another significant statement because this subject is one that should be of concern to every hon. member. This tendency has been a general tendency. When can we better discuss it, when can we better reverse the trend, than when we see it carried to this extreme point in this way? In a comparatively recent book entitled "Government by Decree" written by M. A. Sieghart we find these words, which have a direct application to what is under discussion:
The democratic method of law-making by a representative assembly is being superseded in many fields by the autocratic method of government legislation. Though this legislation is delegated and controlled by parliament, it can no longer be described as subordinate as it is usually equipped with the force of law. Owing to the

-wide discretionary powers conferred by the instruments of authority, it also enjoys to a great extent immunity from judicial control.
The government is thus being instituted as a second legislature and the ordinance changed into a law Whatever are the reasons for these changes it would be futile to minimize the dangers which result from the present lack of constitutional balance. These dangers are real dangers, despite the fact that they are so far not of an actual, but of a potential danger only.
Those words might have been written to apply directly to the problem now before us, but the very fact that those words were written in relation to the general problem of delegated authority indicates that members opposite need not be sensitive when we discuss this subject, when we argue that the time has come for all members to recognize what they are doing, and that this legislation provides the best possible opportunity that may ever be afforded to us to reverse this dangerous trend. Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was discussing the effect of section 30. I must confess that I found it most difficult to believe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did not fully understand the application of section 30. From the interjections he made I would suggest that it is most important that he examine section 30 most carefully. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who sometimes displays, as to the legal aspects of certain documents, knowledge which indicates perhaps that his earlier training might have been other than it actually was, seemed to be under the impression that it was necessary that there be some unusual circumstances before section 30 would apply. With his continuous interjections I found it a little difficult to believe that he was being serious, but I now can see that probably he was. He seemed to have the idea that it was necessary that there be some unusual demands in relation to defence before section 30 would be applied. That section reads:
The governor in council may, from time to time, (a) designate as an essential material any material or substance the control of the supply and use of which is, in his opinion, essential to ensure the availability of adequate defence supplies or for the construction or operation of defence projects:
That does not suggest that any unusual situation must exist. It does seem to me that this is an appropriate time to point out that when we are discussing national defence we are not discussing a subject that is unusual. On the other hand, we are discussing the most definite basic subject which becomes the responsibility of any government or of any parliament. The first and most demanding responsibility of any government within organized society is to assure the defence of that society. That has been true from the beginning of history. In the minds of all of us there is unquestionably the hope that circumstances will be such that the need for defence will be as limited as possible. Nevertheless, I do not know of a single nation in the world large or small which has not recognized the responsibility for defence. Therefore the need of obtaining defence supplies is a continuing [Mr. Drew.)
need which lies at the very root of the continuing responsibility of any government in the ordinary aspects of society.
It is not an international emergency; it is not a domestic emergency; it is simply ordinary demands, and that is what this is. This is not emergency powers, this is something corresponding to the War Measures Act. This is the Defence Production Act; an act to call for the production of defence material. There have been times when we were in the happy position that only a relatively small amount needed to be spent on defence, but there has not been a day since Canada became a nation in 1867 that defence supplies of some kind were not required. Therefore it is a continuing responsibility.
All that the government needs to do to invoke the powers of section 30 is to designate at any time any material as being essential for defence purposes. There need be no declared emergency, such as a war. There need be no appeal to any other act on the statute books. The government needs only to declare that any material is an essential material for the purposes of defence production. Then in the case of services it provides:
*overnor " council may, from time to time, (0) designate as an essential service the carrying on of any commercial activity, including the generation and distribution of electrical energy, the control of which is, in his opinion, essential for the adequate production or use of essential materials for defence supplies or defence projects.
That means that anything that would go into the fabrication, the power needed for fabrication, or any stage of the production of the kind of defence material we would need at any time could be declared without any special declaration of any kind as an essential service by the government. That is the scope of this power. It was in relation to that wide power that I pointed out that there could be no possible question from the legal point of view that the inclusion of the generation and distribution of hydroelectric energy not only brought the generation and distribution of hydroelectric energy within the application of section 30, but that by the use of the ejusdem generis rule of law every other production of power or the production of coal, or, if you will, of atomic energy, or anything else that would go into the necessary industrial activities associated with defence production, or anything that would be of service in the nature of defence production, could be brought under the control of the government. That being the case, it is not necessary to state that any particular thing is going to be done. I repeat, I do not believe that any person with any appreciation of

the application of these statutes could reasonably question the fact that the control of the handling of gas and oil, the construction of pipe lines, the terms under which the gas and oil would be handled by those pipe lines and all other arrangements could be brought under the control of the government just as could hydroelectric generation and distribution.
Whether that is the intention or not, the obligation of all hon. members is not to say in their minds, as was said by the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press in the editorial to which I referred this morning, that we should try to understand the motives of the government. That is not our responsibility on this side or on the other side of the house. Our responsibility is not to place on the statute books any laws which in themselves create a situation that would be contrary to the fundamental and tested principles of parliamentary government. That is exactly what we are dealing with here; not with what any one of us might think this minister or any other minister may do, but rather what this minister or any other minister could do, and particularly what some minister in the distant future, who has had no part in this discussion and who might have an entirely different concept of the organization of our society from that which most of us share, might do when he found he had the powers conferred upon him by this act.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must examine section 30, not only from the point of view of the dangerously wide powers conferred, but also from the constitutional point of view. The essential services and the essential supplies covered by section 30 are services and supplies that in the ordinary course of events would be exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. We know from the case to which I referred this morning, decided in privy council in 1946, that if an act of parliament is passed here which is accepted as being within the wide interpretation of peace, order and good government, as was the Canada Temperance Act passed in 1878, once that becomes law and enters our statutes then it overrides provincial jurisdiction. It did in the case of the Canada Temperance Act, and it would in this case. Therefore, this section directly overrides the jurisdiction of the provincial governments over property and civil rights, as well as over resources and matters of that kind which are so exclusively within their power.
Do not let any hon. member shake his head and raise any question as to whether that is the case. Whether or not it is exercised is another matter; but whether it is exercised
Defence Production Act or not, the powers are conferred by this act to override our constitution. It was for that reason that I said before, and for that reason I repeat, that this act without any time limit, without any restraint, without any of the elimination of the unnecessary powers to which the minister himself referred as recently as March, properly should be called an act to suspend the Canadian constitution. That is exactly what it is. Whether or not the powers are exercised, the powers remain. The adoption of this measure without time limit, without any pretence that it relates to a special emergency, embedding, as it would, in the permanent law of Canada these wide powers, would be a retrograde step from which it might be extremely difficult for this parliament to return at some future time.
Some hon. members might ask why it might be difficult. I know that every hon. member has watched with interest what happened in Britain. They have watched with interest what happened in the case of the nationalization of the steel industry and the nationalization of other activities in that country by a socialist government. They know that, once this nationalization takes place, the unscrambling of the mess created is not something that is very easy to accomplish. With all the effort that has been made, it has been extremely difficult for a government which believes in free enterprise to end the chaos created by the nationalization brought about by the socialist government in Britain. We should not say to ourselves that we do not need to worry because we believe in the minister and he would be doing this. Ask yourselves whether it can be done; and, if it can be done, then ask yourselves if in good conscience you can put on the statute books legislation that would produce that result which some person who happened at some time in the future, even in the very distant future, to have the opportunity could bring about. Let us remember that we are now asked to pass an amendment which would have the effect of embedding this statute in the statute books for any length of time. We know what happened in the case of the Canada Temperance Act. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) is gratified by the fact that it is still there; but there are those who feel that confusion arose between that act and some of the provincial acts. Nevertheless, whether it is right or whether it is wrong we know that, as the result of the decisions which have been made, the courts will hold that this act would be effective if it were passed. In order to make any of these things effective, offences are provided; and when we look at the offences we find that a number of these offences are not offences against known law. Here is where the rule of law comes in. Surely if there is one thing that is the pride of our system, it is that every Canadian shall know, in advance, what he can or cannot do under laws that he can understand. There is an old saying that ignorance of the law is no defence. That is a difficult enough thing, but surely it is doubly difficult when it is not a matter of even orders in council which must be published in the ordinary way but when the situation is that even ministers' orders can create offences which can produce quite serious consequences. In section 32 we find this:

Then, paragraph (e) reads: contravenes or fails to observe any provision of this act or any order or regulation not mentioned in paragraphs (a) to (d).
That means that any of the orders under all these sections I have mentioned would be dealt with under this section. The minister orders, and he does not even carry it out himself but appoints a controller and that controller may carry it into effect. All these offences can be created by some person untrained for the task, without any special knowledge, and simply because he happens to think that something should be done.
Then we find under section 32, subsection 2, the following:
Every person guilty of an offence under paragraph (a) of subsection 1 is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, and if the failure to make the return of which he is convicted continues after the conviction he is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding two hundred dollars for each day on which the failure continues . . .

Then, section 32, subsection 3, reads:
Every person guilty of an offence under this act, other than an offence mentioned in subsection two, is liable upon summary conviction or conviction upon indictment to a fine not exceeding
. thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years or to both fine and imprisonment.
Now, those are severe penalties, and penalties which should not be imposed on Canadian citizens except under laws that are clearly defined.
I know, Mr. Speaker, there have been interjections suggesting that we have overlooked the fact there are administrative laws in this country, not only of this government but provincial legislatures. Of course there are. In the complex society in which we live there has grown up a necessity for what is known as administrative law. But that administrative law can be defined and that administrative law can provide some procedure by which the government assumes responsibility. The fact that any of those things may have been done in the past, in this house or in any other house, is no answer to the proposition to which we have been directing attention, the dangers ahead. The time has come to get back to the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. There will be no better time for any of us to assert that principle than right now when this amendment is before us that would embed this statute in our continuing law.
Let us look at section 37. It reads:
No controller or investigator is responsible at law for any act or thing done by him in good faith in the performance of his duties or the exercise of his powers under this act and no action may be taken against a controller or investigator in respect thereof but nothing in this section limits or restricts the rights of any person against the crown.
The fact that there is a right of action against the crown is no satisfactory answer to the fact that these controllers or investigators, any Tom, Dick or Harry, appointed not by the present Minister of Defence Production but any minister of defence production now or 50 years from now, cannot be sued no matter how wrong their actions as long as they were committed in good faith. Certainly, that is going much too far. So far as this is concerned, the whole problem that is before us is whether or not we should delegate powers to a minister and the minister to people about whom we know nothing, about whom the government will know nothing and then, in turn, simply because in their ignorance of the law, they had acted in good faith in doing something very wrong, there is no right of action against them. That is exactly what this says. This invites careless and improper acts. Do not let it be suggested that careless and improper acts have not taken place.
There has been a gratifying increase of interest that has been indicated this afternoon. I am hoping that interest will increase. Nothing could be more gratifying to those who have been seeking to impress the importance of this upon parliament than the way in which we have been urged by hon. members opposite to continue with our discussion on this subject. There is good reason why that should be done.

This is an erosion of the very foundation of our laws. When Mr. Clement Davies was dealing with this subject he was not, of course, dealing with an act that went nearly as far as the one that is now before us. Hon. members have shown their interest in the effect of this, but when hon. members seem to feel that there is no real danger in a matter of this kind, may I point out that there was one of the most illuminating cases that occurred in Britain last year. It should be read by everyone who is being called upon to pass judgment in this case. I had pointed out the extent to which this act not only creates government by decree, by order in council, but also government by decree by a minister who, in turn, can turn over the whole responsibility to people whose names are unknown. I am sorry the minister is not present at the time I raise this particular case because it is one that has a very direct bearing upon this subject.
The case to which I refer is known as the Crichel Down case, and it was a perfect example of what happens when powers are delegated to those who have no direct responsibility to parliament. Of course, in the Crichel Down case, it was civil servants who are under an oath of office and not just any person without any responsibility either to the government or to parliament. Nevertheless the Crichel Down case was a very illuminating case, and one which should be in the mind of each member when he is asked to vote for wide-open provisions of this kind.
Defence Production Act
In that case the situation that led to the inquiry last year arose out of the fact that some 725 acres of land were taken over by the air ministry of Great Britain in 1940 to be used as a bombing range. This was done under the wide-open powers exercised during the war. When that bombing range was required no longer, then the property was transferred to the ministry of agriculture. In due course it was decided that these lands should be used for agricultural purposes. That was not an unreasonable thing for the ministry of agriculture to decide.
Then the question came up as to how they were to deal with these lands. A number of people wanted the opportunity to take the separate parcels which had made up that 725 acres. There were, in fact, four parcels that had been brought together under that single holding.
One of those who were applying for consideration was the husband of a lady who actually had inherited a right in the property. Therefore there was a special reason why his application should be considered.
Not only were these applications not given due consideration but they were treated with arrogance which did bring this to the attention of members of the government. As a result the government appointed a committee of inquiry-rather I should say they appointed Sir Andrew Clark, O.C., to conduct an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding this case. Sir Andrew Clark's report is a commentary upon what happens in any case of this kind. And I submit that the whole report, which can be found here in our very excellent library, could well be read by every hon. member before he should consider himself ready to vest these wide powers in the minister in this case.
Sir Andrew Clark explained it was difficult to understand the trend that led the officials of the department of agriculture to act in the offensive and arrogant way they did. He then pointed out that there were certain reasons why people who had applied should have been heard; and these are his words, in part, which I quote from this extended report:
It appears difficult at first sight to see how such a misconception could ever have arisen. It had, however, been the fixed policy of the socialist government never to sell any land that had been acquired by the government, whether compulsorily or otherwise, except under very special circumstances, and presumably this policy had become so firmly established that many civil servants were under the impression that there was no power to sell.
Sir Andrew Clark then reviewed the attitude of hostility shown by officials to those who were trying to obtain their land, and

Defence Production Act particularly to the application of Commander Marten, whose wife had a direct interest in one of the business properties. I submit that his words are significant when we are considering what we are being asked to do here in re-creating these wide powers which can be exercised at any time if the government so decides. This was what he said:
There was no excuse whatever for this attitude. Lieutenant Commander Marten acted perfectly properly throughout and was merely endeavouring to stand up for what he conceived to be his moral rights. This attitude was engendered solely by a feeling of irritation that any member of the public should have the temerity to oppose or even question the acts or decisions of officials of a government or state department.
Mr. Speaker, it is just like the minister himself in this instance. The minister does not think we should have the temerity to question what he asks, so he has left the chamber and is not even listening. But I am hoping that someone in his place will refer the Crichel Down case to him.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is of course one very interesting aspect of this because in the Crichel Down case there had been no wrongdoing of any kind. It was just a misconception of duty. There had been arrogance to the public. There had been the highly improper conduct of those who resented even the thought that any member of the public would question their lofty words. And, as Sir Andrew Clark said:
This attitude was engendered solely by a feeling of irritation that any member of the public should have the temerity to oppose or even question the acts or decisions of officials of a government or state department.
Now, the minister had nothing to do with it; the minister did not even know it. But Sir Thomas Dugdale, who was minister of agriculture, felt himself compelled to resign, without request, because at Westminster they have respect for the rights of the people and they have respect for the rights of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, if the same principle applied here we would see at least half the government changing overnight because of a situation of that kind. But of course the same principles do not apply. We have had the explanation here that the conscience of the individual member is his own conscience, and that they all go their own sweet way as they see fit. But at Westminster they have a sterner code. And therefore Sir Thomas Dugdale felt compelled to resign from the government because within his department there had been an attitude toward the public that was utterly impossible.
