I am going to go ahead; hon. members do not have to encourage me. I am going to go ahead. But I do welcome the invitation, because this is the most important principle we will have to discuss, whether unlimited powers ought to be conferred, not merely on the government but on a minister, or anyone he wishes to delegate.
It was Edmund Burke who said:
The people never give up their liberties but under some delusion.
Many hon. members opposite originally- I am inclined to hope they are not so inclined now-were under the delusion that this act did not transgress the basic principles of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. I hope that many of them have changed their opinion in regard to that. It is unquestionably true that the acceptance of improper legislation is not done by people who intend deliberately to do wrong. On the contrary it is done by people who think they are doing right. And in these last few years, in the name of efficiency and expediency, much has been put on the statute books of this and other countries by people of different parties-and let me emphasize that-in the belief that there would be a more expeditious way of doing it.
An effort has been made to create the delusion that this act is necessary to provide our defence requirements. Well, it has not been necessary once in the last two years; and yet hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on defence requirements. If that is so, then let us know just exactly what circumstances would call for the exercise of these wide powers, not included in that act already on the statute books, which gives very wide powers indeed and, as the minister has pointed out, does go very far in conferring powers both on the government and on the minister.
Whether that is right or not, at least it is on the statute books; and we would be making a move in the right direction by stopping with an act that continued the Department of Defence Production and then relied upon an ordinary act for the purchase of supplies, such as has been found adequate in similar jurisdictions.
The necessity for weapons of defence is one which need not be emphasized. Everybody believes in that. Everybody believes that this should be done upon an expeditious and proper basis. And, make no mistake about it that, so far as the members of this party are concerned, we do not believe that there should be any profiteering out of the production of those things made necessary by the desperate demands of defence in a time like this.

Nevertheless, having said that, never should patriotism be an excuse for a break-down of our basic parliamentary democracy. Democracy begins at home. We are at this time being asked to support tremendous expenditures for the defence of this country, this democratic system of ours, for the right of our people to live under a parliamentary democracy.
If it is worth while to create armed forces, and if it is worth while to spend the enormous amounts that are being spent for that purpose, then, Mr. Speaker, I submit it is proper for us to consider a way in which we can assure the continuance of that parliamentary democracy right here in the first line of democracy, the House of Commons of Canada.
That is what is actually before us, just a simple act, two sentences: one, to change the salary of the minister, something that at the moment is not needed. Of course, the very fact they are doing that indicates they have another minister in mind, because the present minister is paid as Minister of Trade and Commerce. Therefore, it is quite clear that they are preparing for some other minister in this position. We do not know who it is. That is of course something that is not vouchsafed to us. I do not imagine that even hon. members opposite, who are called upon to vote, have been told who that other minister will be. In fact, it would be contrary to our principles of government if they were informed in advance. There may be quite a number of them who would hope that they might be chosen. It is a perfectly legitimate hope. Probably some of us might hope that a certain number of individuals would be considered for that post while this government still has that responsibility; but in any event it is perfectly clear that if this government thought there was going to be no change in the minister they would not even bother about that amendment because the present minister is paid as Minister of Trade and Commerce and of course cannot receive a second salary. Therefore, the very fact there is the amendment emphasizes the fact that, so far as their confidence in the present minister is concerned, it is someone else they have in mind when they are dealing with this legislation.
It is the second section that raises the fundamental and only principle involved. Shall powers which were temporary, shall powers which were described as recently as March of this year by the Minister of Defence Production as being powers which should not be continued, without any amendment be continued to an indefinite date in
Defence Production Act the future? Shall they become permanent on the statute books of Canada? That is the issue. There has not been a greater issue before the House of Commons since this house was set up under the British North America Act in 1867.
I regret that the minister is not present. The Minister of Defence Production interjected this morning, "Of course, the hon. member says there is no emergency." I say nothing of the kind. There is an emergency of the kind that always exists when conflicting powers are being built up. There was no doubt about it that there were many people who thought they were living in a period of emergency in Britain during the time that the wars with France went on for hundreds of years. There is no doubt about it, there was a feeling of emergency in Britain at the time that the Armada approached the British shores. There is no doubt about it that there have been many occasions since then when the people of Britain thought there was something in the nature of an emergency. But there is a vast difference between that and the kind of compelling emergency such as suddenly arises at the outbreak of a war when the ordinary activities are disputed, and when the ordinary supplies are not available. But that is a different thing from what we have today. In the years before the first world war and in the years before the two world wars great forces were being built up. Nobody was in any doubt that there were two conflicting forces growing in the world in the years before the two world wars, and particularly after 1933 when Hitler came into power in Germany. Everyone knew that, but we did not put on the statute books in Canada broad powers of this kind to be forever embedded in our legislation to by-pass parliament and to leave every individual Canadian in uncertainty as to what his legal rights were in the carrying on of his daily duties. We did not put on the statute books laws that permeated into every aspect of our society; we did not pass laws then which were regarded by the socialists as entirely in keeping with their own desires for a planned economy and the opportunity to exercise control over every aspect of that economy.
Our socialist friends are perfectly sincere in this; we know that it is part of their doctrine; it is part of their idea. But this is the first time that we have that idea declared so openly in support of a measure of this kind that has been placed before the house by the government itself.
If at this time when we have reached as high a measure of stability in the international field as we shall reach for many long years

Defence Production Act to come, if at this time, when the representatives of the 60 nations which signed the United Nations charter are now gathered at San Francisco to commemorate that event with some measure of satisfaction about the stability that has been attained, if at this time we cannot return to the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law, then it is difficult to imagine when, in the lifetime of any one of us, that possibility will ever present itself.
Yes, there is an emergency, a very real emergency, but it is not the emergency suggested by the Minister of Defence Production. The emergency is the threat to our freedom, to the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law-what Clement Davies said, the steady erosion of the basic principles of parliament itself. It is for that we are fighting; it is for that we shall continue to fight, no matter what happens.

I ask this house the same question I have asked myself many times. Do we want a minister, a representative of the people, to exercise essential powers in an emergency, or are we prepared to leave those essential powers to be exercised by the great industrialists of this country, no matter how well intentioned they are? Let me give you some examples, as the Leader of the Opposition gave you some examples. Let us take the field of electronics, a very important field. Many important and essential patents are now in use. We need them. If we do not have them, they can well retard our defence effort and in some cases nullify it.
Is there anyone who will say we do not need the power to take and use these patents and to compensate people for them? It is needless for me to recite all these editorials that have appeared in the press across Canada. They do, Mr. Speaker, I think, share the concern that we in our party feel if such a bill as this is finally enacted.
Perhaps I need refer to only one or two. Naturally I shall not do more than just comment on what the editorials say. I refer in particular to the one in the Ottawa Citizen, which is a newspaper well known to be quite friendly to the present government of this country. This editorial seems to emphasize the fact there is no need now to lay down a permanent policy based upon a permanent crisis. When the hon. member for Spadina was speaking in his usually impressive form, he did not dwell on what I thought was the crux of this debate; that is, the need for a time limit. I quite agree with most of what he said, and I am going to comment on some of his remarks. He did not mention our main complaint, the fact that there is no

time limit. The press of this country is complaining about that, too; let there be no mistake about that.
The Citizen goes on to say that these are not the kind of regulations suitable for the Canadian economy. I think every member in the house, regardless of party, must have high regard for a statement of that sort coming from an editorial writer who supports the Liberal party in this country. Let us not overlook this statement, which appeared in that same editorial, that Canadians should be given some assurance that they are not slipping a little at a time into a state-controlled economy. I am sure the Liberals in this house do not share the views our socialist friends have. I hope most of them do not, though I believe the socialists have been referred to by some leaders of the Liberals as Liberals in a hurry. Certainly they are supporting the government on this bill because it is right down their alley.
This article in the Citizen, which is so forcible and well written, I think is one that represents the viewpoint of many people in this dominion. It goes on to say that it might be fair to grant an extension of powers such as those in this Defence Production Act for a year, two years, or three years. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is what the members of my party have been asking for since the opening of this debate. We make no apology to anybody for carrying on this debate, because we are sincere in our efforts and we do hope, before the debate is concluded, that the government will finally realize they have made a mistake. We hope the government will put a time limit on this measure.
In the early part of his remarks the hon. member for Spadina said that his party reflects public opinion. I am going to say here and now that there is no party in this house that has a mandate from the people to give any one minister the powers that would be conferred by this bill. He said it was all or nothing and he quoted a song, I think, "I've got plenty of nothing".
Then, he went on to ask, can we afford to be unprepared? We agree with that; we cannot afford to be unprepared. We are not objecting to the money that is being devoted to defence expenditures in order that together with our allies we may preserve some sort of system in this world. We do not object to defence expenditures. We would like to have a better accounting of them than we are allowed to get. All we want is value for the money spent, and the taxpayers in the country expect to get value for the money spent. We need to be prepared, and we agree with that. We have said so from the
Defence Production Act beginning of this debate; we have said so ever since I have been a member of this party whenever defence expenditures came up for deliberation.
I regret to say that this afternoon the hon. member for Spadina, who is a very good friend of mine and one of the most capable members of this house, made an effort to confuse the issue, but he did not succeed. He said the government wants power to ensure a continuous supply of materials. We do not disagree with that. Why should he quarrel with that idea or throw it to the house as an original idea, except as part of his argument to confuse the issue? We never did oppose a continuous supply of materials, and we never shall. He asks whether we want the minister to direct industry, or whether we want industry to take over. Well, now, in an emergency we expect that the emergency powers will be used. Let there be no mistake about that. We expect this government or any government in power during an emergency to have the power to give direction. Our complaint is, and it will be until this debate is finished, that the government should not have those powers on a permanent basis.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Are there not going to be any more elections?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Oh, we had
one in Ontario the other day, and the C.C.F. lost a lot of ground.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What will the Tories think about it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The Tories got over 80 members. As a matter of fact I should like to see another election tomorrow, and I am going to say something about elections later.
The hon. member for Spadina said they wanted the right to obtain strategic materials. Did we say that any minister should not have the right? Are we attacking any minister or any government because of the right to obtain strategic materials. The hon. member said they wanted the power to investigate. We are willing that they should have the power to investigate, but we do not want those snoopers around such as we had during the last war, who were about as well qualified to perform their duties as-I shall not make any comparison, Mr. Speaker, because sometimes you have to call me to order for my conservative expressions. He says they may want copper from Chile. We are quite willing that the minister have the power to get all the copper he wants from any nation. As a matter of fact we are producing many raw

Defence Production Act materials today in this country that we would like to sell. We would like to have the government use them.
The hon. member says there has been an endless debate on this bill, and he objects to the continuation of the debate. He says the purpose is to divide the cabinet. Let me tell him that the cabinet is "frozen in futility and divided in disunity". Let there be no mistake about that. I sometimes wonder-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Every member of the cabinet now in the house thinks the same way.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Yes; you
mean about being divided. Well, we have one minister of the crown in the chamber at the present time, and for a while this afternoon we had two of them. During the course of the debate we have certainly had one part of the time, but the other ministers do not seem to feel called upon to be here.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You could not blame them for not listening to this drivel.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It is common gossip that they do not seem to be in accord so far as this bill is concerned. However, the minister is determined, as his last and final act, to get this thing through. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I'll be here after you are, brother.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
You and I
have been here together quite a while. I acknowledge and respect the ability of the minister. We have had quite a few clashes, but that does not take away from my respect for him. In fact he helps me out; and I hope at the next election he will come down to my riding and have me introduce him.
But as I look across at the treasury benches I am wondering what the minister has in mind. To whom is he going to give these powers? I cannot see anyone, with perhaps one exception. It may be that there is one over there who would like to take over from the present minister, and that is of course the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) who slithered onto the government benches off the slippery bow of a fishing boat on the east coast. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It will not be you.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Oh, I am not
concerned about you little fellows from Ontario. You got your licking the other day. However, there is nothing I like better than to be interrupted.
I was referring to the responsibilities of this portfolio, and who will take over. Apparently the Minister of Defence Production is not to be the one, because it is common gossip that he will quit in October.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Wishful thinking.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
This is a
strange measure-

speechtext: You will be wrong again.

speechtext:

Coming back to these degrees required by a minister to take over such responsibility, I hope I may be permitted to tell a joke which concerned Hon. George W. Ross. Some of the lawyers in the house may appreciate it. He was called before the law society and, in passing, it will be recalled that he was at one time the distinguished leader of a political party in Ontario. When called before the law society he was to be given the degree of bachelor of law. Hon. members will keep in mind that this is just a story, and that it may or may not be true. When called before the benchers of the law society they said, "Sir George, you will have to answer questions asked by the benchers of the law society." He said, "Yes, I agree to do that". The treasurer, who was chairman, said, "Mr. Ross, what do you know about law?" To this Mr. Ross replied, "I don't know a damn thing about law." So it was recorded in the annals of the law society that Sir George, having appeared before the law society and having been questioned and having answered correctly, was given the degree of LL.D.
I just had that in mind when the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was boasting about the degrees he had, and I was wondering if he was the one the Minister of Defence Production had in mind. But he is not the only minister in the cabinet who would want these powers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Is this the library bill we are discussing?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We in this party are prepared to see that a department

of government has the necessary power to take care of our defence purchasing. We admit as readily as anybody else that we are not facing a pleasant situation today. It is unfortunate that we have to spend two billion dollars each year for defence, but we cannot help it. We are hopeful that this may not be a permanent condition. However, while it exists we are prepared to admit that some department of government should have the power necessary to keep us in a position where we can accept our proper responsibilities as one of the allies for the preservation of democracy in this world.
I have been greatly surprised at the change shown by the C.C.F. since the resolution was introduced. I believe it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who said, as reported at pages 1996 and 1997 of Hansard, that there should be a time limit. I am not quoting exactly but I believe that is what he said, in substance. We in the official opposition, after making the proposal to the government that there should be a time limit, expected the government would pay some attention. If it had, this debate would not be continuing as it is now. Naturally we would object to some of the proposals in the bill.
Our objections were fully covered with exceptional skill by the hon. member for Eglinton and again today by the Leader of the Opposition. I do not intend to deal at length with those matters at the moment, but in common with other members of this party I object to the dictatorial powers set out in the bill. While I do not intend to comment in detail, I would call attention to section 5 of the act, where it says:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Then section 7 (3) is one which must concern many hon. members and many people throughout Canada. It says:
The minister may remove any members, directors or officers of a corporation incorporated under this section at any time and may appoint others in their stead or may appoint additional persons as members.
True, he has never exercised such powers in the past; but there they are. There is the pattern, set according to the C.C.F. philosophy, which would certainly be adopted by them if they ever formed a government, although we share the opinion of hon. members in the Liberal party that they will never have that opportunity.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Yes.
Defence Production Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The section from which the member has quoted says the minister may remove directors. In privately owned companies the shareholders and the owners may remove directors. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, in this particular section there is nothing the minister cannot do.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
So many sections of this bill give the minister power instead of the cabinet that I am quite sure it must be very disturbing to thinking people of this country. In section 9 exclusive authority is given the minister to buy or otherwise acquire defence supplies and construct defence projects required by the Department of National Defence, and so on. Section 15 is rather amazing. The minister has power to acquire, utilize, store, transport, sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of defence supplies.
Without any doubt this bill is a challenge to the Conservative party. I am saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that we Conservatives are not going to be content to sit idly by and watch the twilight of freedom darken into a totalitarian night under this or any other government which advocates such ideas and gives such powers to any minister.
This minister demands all or nothing, in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister has said there should be a time limit. The Minister of Defence Production has also said there should be a time limit, but apparently

Defence Production Act a change has come about in somebody's thinking. It certainly must be in the minister's, because he defies his own cabinet, he defies his own Prime Minister and he defies parliament. He says, "I will tell you when this thing is going to be terminated; nobody is going to tell me, including my own Prime Minister". That is on the record, Mr. Speaker. I do not like to see that sort of thing on the record; I do not like to see that kind of remark made by any minister, whether he be a junior or senior minister.
I challenge this government. I say to them, if you think you have a mandate to pass this bill giving the minister such dictatorial powers, go to the country and get a mandate. I challenge you now, go to the country, have an election, and let the people tell you whether you are going to give one minister such dictatorial powers as are contained in the Defence Production Act. Go to the country. You will come back, but you will not form the government, I tell you that. You claimed a moment ago that you had a mandate. You have no mandate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If we did that you would not have a corporal's guard.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: There is more of a smokescreen than fire in this speech.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I like comments such as that from the little member for Halifax. I respect his interruptions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: He is the senior junior.

speechtext:
Is that it?
Before I conclude my remarks I want to put this on the record. I have challenged the government to go to the country. Get going. The last time you had an election in August. Have this one in September; any time after September 16 would be fine. If hon. members opposite have not read the July issue of the Reader's Digest I hope they get it, because I am going to read a little excerpt from it. It will be found on page 53. This was written by Curtis Bok, and reads as follows:
In one of his books, Curtis Bok recounted the historical fact that in one section of ancient Greece it was long the custom that when a man proposed a law in the popular assembly, he did so on a platform with a rope around his neck.

This is in quotation marks:
If his law passed, they removed the rope; and if it failed, they removed the platform.
The minister is determined to get all these powers. I never saw anybody so eager for something which was not necessary as the minister is for these particular powers. It reminds me of the statement of a squaw.
I am not comparing the minister with a squaw, but when she was talking about whisky she said: "A little too much is just right."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Next joke, please.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax must have got that. I knew the others would not catch it. The minister is hiding behind the skirts of the Prime Minister. He comes to this house like the ancient Athenian, standing on a platform with a rope around his neck. He says it is all or nothing. He says: "I will decide the emergency." In other words, he says "I live or die as a public figure on the proposition that this act must be accepted in toto or rejected in toto." That is what it is.
My esteem of the minister is already on record. Most of the speeches that have been made by members of the Liberal party have added nothing but praise of the minister, and of course that is repetition. Since I am already on record concerning my esteem for him, I do not need to repeat it. What we must keep in mind is that while we have a high regard for a particular person, the same person can make a lot of mistakes and the minister himself is no exception. As a matter of fact, for years he argued that crown companies should not be taxed, or they should not make payments in lieu of taxes. He did that persistently, perhaps because I was the only member in the house who advocated it. Finally he was apparently overruled by his associates. They had more effect then than they have today, because in 1949 the government introduced a formula respecting crown companies which concerned the Minister of Defence Production inasmuch as it was exactly contrary to his persuasive eloquence and opinions for years prior.
As a result of the formula which was announced by the government, this year the city of Sarnia will probably get $280,000. He was certainly wrong then, because the government adopted the formula which should have been adopted years before. The same minister certainly cannot claim he was right with respect to the arguments we had in this house concerning sugar beets some two or three years ago, when his temper flared and he was quite white, as he usually is when attacked; and at that time he was much perturbed.

As a matter of fact, we do not have to go back that far, Mr. Speaker. I had a resolution on the order paper calling for the setting up of a committee on research, suggesting that the government should accelerate research in this country. A year ago I did not have the opportunity to discuss it because of collaboration in the house. On February 3 the same minister to whom we are asked to give all these powers today said, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), "We shall set up a committee on atomic energy and research generally." He put the motion on the order paper but a few days ago said they are not going to set up the committee, and blamed the opposition for it.
The committee could have been set up in February, and it could have been set up a year ago. I realize, I am complimented to think, that the government recognized my arguments over the years for this research committee and more research in Canada when the minister put on the order paper the motion to set up a committee on research and atomic energy.
Of course that is not relevant to this debate. I cannot discuss anything about research.
I was glad to note that the Minister of Finance indicated in his budget speech that a royal commission to study the economy of this country would be set up. Only the other day the Prime Minister announced the membership of that commission. It is important to appreciate that the functions of that commission will be very important, and as a matter of fact are what we had in mind in asking for a committee on research.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The hon. member prefaced his remarks by saying he would be out of order if he discussed research, and then he proceeded to do so. I think he has been extended every latitude and perhaps now he might come back to the principle of this bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The hon. member is just normally confused.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I am glad I am not like the hon. member. He says I am normally confused, but I would much rather be that than be abnormally confused. His interpretation reminds me of some eastern philosophy I read a few years ago:
I never saw a purple cow,
I never hope to see one;
But I can tell you, anyhow,
I'd rather see than be one.
I appreciate Your Honour directing my attention to my slight infringement of the 50433-317
Defence Production Act rules. I had hoped as a matter of fact that I might have been infringing the rules from the time I started.
The stand of the official opposition has already been indicated by the hon. member for Eglinton and again today by my leader. Several other members of my party have given our reasons for taking the stand we do. What is alarming to me is that as yet no member on the government side has given any reason why these powers should be granted for an unlimited time. I can understand the C.C.F. supporting this bill, and it is not at all unexpected to see the government members supporting it because when the minister says he wants it they just pop up and do what they are told. It is just the same as when the library bill came up. The minister sponsoring that bill stood up and said he would not accept the amendment. He shook his head, with the hair combed like Hitler's, and then he squirmed, although he does not squirm so much when he is standing up as when he is sitting down.
I asked him how many paintings had been purchased by the national gallery and the minister replied that it would take weeks to find out. I could take two secretaries and any member of the house and get the information in two or three days.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If the hon. member is ready to do that I shall be only too delighted to have him do so.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am glad the minister is so obliging. We want that information.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Send your two secretaries along.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Even with the assistance of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration I think we should not continue with this portion of the debate. I believe we had better get back to the principle of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
These interruptions disturb my continuity of thought. The stand of our party has been amply stated. The war in Korea justified the special defence measures that were taken in 1951. While we opposed the powers that were granted at that time, as Canadian citizens we felt there should be no hesitancy in granting those powers but with a time limit.
Notwithstanding what the minister says, I do not think we are faced today with the crisis we were faced with in 1951. This is borne out by the statements of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)

Defence Production Act and Sir Anthony Eden. The extraordinary powers which are to be conferred upon the minister seem to go beyond what was required in wartime. During the war the War Measures Act was in effect and that conferred almost unlimited powers upon the governor in council.
Several suggestions have been made. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) suggested the other day that certain sections in the act be amended in such a way that some of the extraordinary powers would terminate at a specified time. That suggestion was made previously by other members of our party, but it was worth repeating. He suggested also that the expiry date be advanced by one to three years. The third suggestion put forward was that the act be split so the department could be made permanent-something on which there is general agreement-while the rest of the act would terminate unless periodically renewed by parliament.
We say the emergency is not as great now as it was in 1951. If war did come suddenly we have acts on the statute books to take care of the situation. Even if this act were passed with a time limit and with more limited powers, it would be in effect. Therefore we are not obstructing any action that would have to be taken by this government to put us in a position to accept our proper responsibilities.
There is no real need for the special and extraordinary powers contained in the act. Absolutely no reason has been given why there should not be a time limit if the act is continued. The unavoidable conclusion is that the real reason for this bill is the determination of the minister to hold on indefinitely to dictatorial powers.
I say in conclusion that it looks like the minister's last important act is to defy parliament and the other members of the cabinet.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the speech of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) interested me particularly because of the loudness and vigour with which he put forth his challenge to the government to go to the country. My interest arose particularly from the fact that he failed completely to appreciate the humour of the situation. What is more serious is the fact that the subject matter before the house at the moment is not one that warrants humorous treatment. The challenge on the part of the official opposition that the government go to the country now on this issue is not to be taken seriously, but it would be interesting to observe how many of the official opposition would defend the government for calling an election at this time on this issue-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: We would welcome it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: -and go out and explain to the public that it would be a proper use of public funds to have an election on this issue two years after the last election. Near the end of his speech, the hon. member told a great many stories. I confess frankly I was not able to get the point of many of them, but I do not necessarily blame him for that as it may be that I was not equal to finding the humour in them. However, I can claim no distinction for that. It seems that practically every member of the house was in the same position. But he did say that the stand of his party had been amply stated, after some 30 minutes of story telling. I think that is the true position respecting the stand of the party on this bill, as was exemplified from the beginning in the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton. I must tell him that I did him the honour of rereading that speech twice. It took 101 minutes to deliver, and it was not one of the hon. member's better efforts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Some Liberals have told me it was-the real Liberals.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It is notable for its repetition and lack of relevance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It was certainly an effort.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: On the last day this bill was discussed and again today we had the effort of the Leader of the Opposition. I took the trouble to refresh my memory from some notes I made at the time he was speaking, and it is very interesting on analysing that speech to note how much time the hon. gentleman-who does hold an honourable position in this house as Leader of the Opposition, a position which I respect and believe is of real importance under our system-took trying to take advantage of interjections to make smart retorts and irrelevant comments about irrelevant subjects.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What about all the smart and irrelevant interruptions that came from the other side?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
They were not ignored, I can tell you. It is very interesting to see on checking over my notes-and I am sure Hansard will bear me out-that the greater part of that speech was not addressed to the bill but to the rather free-swinging language with the members in general.
That is the privilege of the Leader of the Opposition. It certainly takes up time, and it may be proper for him to use the time he has in debate in that way. He must be the judge of the propriety of using it in that way.

He did at times deal with the bill; he read some of it. I leave that part of his speech with the suggestion that hon. members on all sides of the house check Hansard carefully, and check the Defence Production Act, and note the number of times the limiting clause in the relevant section was omitted. I am quite sure that if hon. members do that, they will dispose of the effort of the Leader of the Opposition very quickly.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Give us those clauses.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I shall come to some of the specific sections in a few minutes. I am quite sure that while we heard from him a great deal about the supremacy of parliament, no effort was made to relate the bill to any breach of that principle.
We noted at the same time his appeal directly to the press, not through the Speaker. That, again, is his privilege. If he wishes to do that, he may. I still think it is not quite a parliamentary method, but if he chooses to use it, it is quite proper to do so. But I am quite sure if those same editors to whom he addressed so many of his remarks, and whose opinions he valued so highly, will read his remarks when they have a copy of the act before them, and read those parts of the sections he quoted as against the whole sections from which he was quoting, they will know how to deal with him, and will be able to deal with him much more effectively than I could deal with him.
I feel that the treatment of this subject has gotten out of context altogether. It is not one that should be batted back and forth as a jocular subject. I could not help noting from the interjections of the official opposition and from reading and listening to the remarks of many who spoke, that they seemed to be thinking about defence procurement in terms of the first great war. It was so apparent that they had not brought their thinking about what is involved in defence procurement up to date. The speaker immediately preceding me spoke about an abundance of materials in this country which one can now buy readily. However, defence procurement is no longer a matter of buying ready-made goods off the shelf. It is a vast enterprise involving the organization of industry for the production of very complex and very involved equipment.
I am frank to tell hon. members that I have found it very difficult on occasion to appreciate the complexity of some of the equipment. Perhaps no better illustration of that can be found than in the matter of ship procurement. It used to be that one 50433-3174
Defence Production Act looked mainly at a hull, and it was another shipbuilding job. Now there is such a mass of electronic equipment involved that certainly any limited comprehension I have of a technical subject like that is strained to understand even the most elementary things about such equipment. It takes a matter of three years to procure such articles.
The field of radar is one in which Canadians can take very great pride, for the Canadian effort in radar has been not inconsiderable. When you examine into some of the electronic devices and what is required to produce them, you realize that, after an emergency arises or a war begins, it is not just a matter of going out and buying them; it is a matter of intensive effort three or four years preceding the time that equipment is required.
Then when you deal with the procurement of aircraft and examine into the type of metals required, you find a degree of quality required in those metals that was not thought of even in 1951, when this bill was previously up for discussion. Those types of metals are neither developed nor produced, nor are the other engineering problems involved in putting them into the finished article worked out after an outbreak of war, if that equipment is to be of any use in any such war.
Then when you deal with the subject of our defence, it is no longer a matter, as it was 30 or 40 years ago, of a declaration of war followed by a slow-moving process, according to today's standards. Two or three times I interjected while he was speaking, as Hansard will indicate, and also during the remarks of earlier speakers, asking what section they felt violated those rules.
It is extremely interesting just to look at the bill and see what is provided, because I could get no answer from them. The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Lambton West made much of section
7.	That section gives the minister-and by the way, any legislation setting up a department gives the minister authority to exercise the power in the name of the department- the right to remove directors of a company or corporation incorporated under the Defence Production Act. It gives him that power. In any company the shareholders pretty well have the power-at least they try to have it-to control. They own the company, and in most companies they have the control. Here we have a public company created for the purpose of carrying out the procurement of certain defence supplies, where the crown or the taxpayers are the owners of the company.
Neither the Leader of the Opposition nor the hon. member for Lambton West, when they attacked the power of the minister to remove any director of such a company, said how they would have the interest of the


public protected. Is that not an extraordinary position to take? Then you go on with some of the other sections of the act, and you find this about the violation of the rule of law. They read section 22 which provides for an appeal to the exchequer court. It reads as follows:
22. (1) A person affected by an order or direction made by the minister under section 21 . . .
And so on. He may appeal to the exchequer court. Where does that provision violate the rule of law? Do not we in this country believe that disputes between citizens or between citizens and the crown are to be settled by the courts? Where is the violation there?
Then they criticize some of the other sections. They talk about section 24, which is another section giving to a person who feels he has a grievance the right to appeal to the exchequer court. So you may go on all the way through the bill and find references, in case of dispute, to the exchequer court. None of the hon. members opposite have pointed out precisely what their objection is to that reference of disputes to the court.
There is one other matter in connection with the bill that I should like to mention. Much has been made of the right of the crown to appoint a controller. A great to-do was made about that matter today by the Leader of the Opposition. I should just like to draw to the attention of hon. members what the Leader of the Opposition omitted to read in dealing with that subject. The hon. member for Greenwood a few days ago, when speaking on the subject, omitted to read it but on that occasion I interjected and had it put on Hansard. Section 27 starts off in this way:
27. (1) Where the minister is satisfied that
(a) a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner.-
Then the powers are given. But that limitation is there. The reference is to a defence contractor who "has failed or is likely to fail".
We on the government side were asked many times by speakers of the official opposition to assume our responsibility under this act. In the light of the difficulties of defence procurement, because of the materials required, I wonder what hon. member is willing today to take away from the government the right to step into the plant of a defence contractor when that defence contractor has failed to deliver the goods? Surely

the position is just the opposite to that stated by the Leader of the Opposition.
Then in the list of powers which the Leader of the Opposition read today, he omitted reference to a similar limitation. Of course that is a rather important omission. If hon. members will look at section 31 they will find that it gives the governor in council certain powers. Section 31 reads:
31. (1) The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he deems necessary to control and regulate the production, processing, distribution, acquisition, disposition or use of essential materials or the supply or use of essential services for the purposes of
(a) ensuring the availability of defence supplies or the construction or operation of defence projects for the defence requirements of Canada and for co-operative arrangements for defence being carried on by Canada and associated governments; . . .
Subsection 2 says-and this was the section the Leader of the Opposition made so much of this morning-
Subject to the regulations, if any, the minister may by order, as he deems necessary for the purposes specified in subsection (1) -
That is the limitation on his powers, and that limitation is not to be found in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition this morning.
A question then arises as to the exercise of the responsibility of a member of the House of Commons. It was quite proper for the Leader of the Opposition to ask members on the government side to be very careful how they exercised their responsibility as members. It was quite a proper appeal, but I wondered why he did not include his own supporters in that appeal.
Let me point out that anyone who considers this subject, and considers it carefully, is not likely to support the stand of the official opposition on this bill. Anyone who does consider that responsibility is likely to want the very best defence procurement we can get in this country. He is going to want, in order to achieve that purpose, the government authority exercising that responsibility to have such powers as will enable him to have all the defence potential of the country mobilized. He is going to want the defence authority exercising that power to have the authority to put in a controller and use the machinery and equipment of any defence contractor who fails to produce as required.
You know, it is a matter of concern these days as to whether we shall have enough defence, and in time. The whole concept of time has changed, and the idea repeatedly expressed in the words of some members of the opposition that "if the emergency arises we will give you the authority" is almost
Defence Production Act pathetic in that it reveals a failure to understand the concept of time necessary in this day and age.
There is one other thing. The language today from the official opposition is a little more moderate. They were concerned about the rights of citizens. Indeed, we had many splendid excerpts from good writers on that subject read to us by members of the opposition. I could not help but wonder why the official opposition, on this bill having to do with the use of property and not with the liberty of the subject, were concerned about the freedom of the individual. If they are sincere, and I must assume that they are, why did they choose this bill that has to do with the use of property-and not the use of property generally but the use of property with respect to defence materials and defence equipment only-as the battleground on which to make their stand? Section 2 (f) (i) of this act, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), reads as follows: Arms, ammunition, implements of war, vehicles, mechanical and other equipment, watercraft, amphibious craft, aircraft, animals, articles, materials, substances and things required or used for the purposes of the defence of Canada or for co-operative efforts for defence being carried on by Canada and an associated government.
That clearly states that animals, at least, are defence supplies, so there we have the first indication that agriculture would be definitely affected. Section 2 (h) reads: "essential material" means a material or substance designated by the governor in council under section 30 as an essential material.
Then we have under section 5 the point to which we take exception, something with which we had some experience during the last war. Farmers generally know best what can be produced on their own farms. It is assumed that the farmer making his living from the land knows best what should be grown and produced there. Yet during the last war there were some instances-not so much here as in other countries, I agree, but we had examples here-of men going around the country telling farmers what they were to grow and when they were to grow it. Those men could not possibly know a farm as well as the farmer himself knew it. In some cases the crop suggested probably could not be grown on that particular farm. Here we have section 5 which reads as follows:
5. The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I say, during the last war we had some experience of officials coming around and telling people what they should do and when they should do it. Is the minister suggesting that he always gets the very best assistants; that he is always able to get assistants who know everything about all farm conditions in Canada, in the various districts, and who could tell better than the farmer himself what should be grown on that particular land? That is what is possible under this act. He could even purchase or expropriate the land under this act, and then put a manager on the farm and direct him as to what should be grown.
Section 9 (2) gives the minister exclusive authority. The section reads as follows:
9. (2) The minister shall have exclusive authority to buy or otherwise acquire defence supplies and [Mr. Charlton.!

construct defence projects required by the Department of National Defence, except
(a) defence projects to be constructed by persons in the employ of Her Majesty, . . .
And so on. Hence it actually gives the minister tremendous powers in so far as the agricultural population are concerned.
Then we have section 23. I suggest that under this section the situation could be disastrous. Under this section the minister can penalize anyone who is storing products for defence purposes. Although we probably have a plentiful supply of wheat at the present moment, a time could come when wheat might not be as plentiful as it is today. It could happen that anyone storing wheat, for instance, would have to take the loss if anything happened to that wheat. I just want to read this section 23:
23. (1) Where a person who has been requested to enter into a defence contract on terms and conditions that the minister considers to be fair and reasonable has refused or failed to enter into the contract, if the minister is satisfied that such person owns or controls facilities that are suitable for or can be adapted to the work required to carry out such contract and that his refusal or failure was without reasonable excuse, the minister may direct that person to produce, deliver or store, or to construct, as the case may be, on such terms and conditions and within such period as the minister considers to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances, the defence supplies or the defence project or projects that would have been the subject-matter of the contract if it had been entered into.
Subsection 2 is the one to which I have direct reference. It reads as follows:
(2) A person who stores defence supplies pursuant to a direction under this section is liable for the loss thereof or for damage thereto as if he had agreed to store them for reward.
A person could be advised or told to store certain perishable products. Then the official might not be around soon enough to tell him when to take them out, and some of those perishable products might spoil. In that case the producer would be expected to take the loss. I suggest that is unfair. Of course I am not suggesting that the minister would do it, but it is a possibility under that act.
Then under section 26, it is worthy of note, a producer could be instructed what to produce on the farm. I know of cases during the last war when sometimes farmers were told they should take their milk to a powdered milk plant instead of sending it to the cheese factory, for instance. In some cases, I know there was no truck going by that farmer's door to the powdered milk plant, whereas there was one going to the cheese factory. That is just an instance of how unreasonable some of these orders can be when all those things are not taken into consideration. I suggest that under this act it is possible to get into troubles of this sort.

Section 26 reads as follows:
26. The governor in council may make such regulations or orders as he deems necessary or advisable to require persons who produce-
That is the word I am pointing out particularly, Mr. Speaker; I refer to the word "produce".
*-or deal in defence supplies or construct defence projects to give priority in the carrying on of their business, in such manner and on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed by or pursuant to the regulations, to the production of or dealing in defence supplies or construction of defence projects to meet the requirements of the defence of Canada or of an associated government.
Ordinarily you do not produce automobiles and you do not produce guns; you manufacture them. However, you do produce food. I therefore suggest that this section would have just as much to do with the production of food as it would with the production of weapons of war.
Then another section that has a good deal of control is section 31, subsection 2. I have a number of sections here, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to read them all or read from them all. But under section 31 it is made plain that the producers would definitely be affected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with all other members of this house, I listened this afternoon with great
Defence Production Act interest, as is our custom, to the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina. He commands, I might say, great respect from all members in this house and his remarks are dealt with in that light.
I was particularly interested in his use of the word "filibuster". He dealt with that word as though it were one of those naughty words that small boys are taught not to use. He dealt with it in much the same way as many people deal with the word "politician". If I disagree with his use of the word, it is perhaps more because of the definition he gave to it. If I correctly interpreted his remarks, and I hope he will correct me if I did not, he said it was obstruction for obstruction's sake. If such is the case, I should like to dissociate myself from the term "filibuster". If on the other hand he is prepared to go along with me and put a slightly different interpretation on the word, namely obstruction or delay for the sake of a principle, then I am quite happy to accept the word "filibusterer" as applied to myself.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, a filibusterer is an adventurer. I have, in times past, read novels of the early years of Christianity, the operations in England and on the seas where, in fact, the word was used to denote an adventurer. In that light I accept the hon. member's condemnation that I am a "filibusterer". In fact, Mr. Speaker, each and every one of us in this house, in all corners of the house, is an adventurer. We are adventurers, I submit, in the interests of democracy and freedom; we are adventurers for Canada. Surely if anyone is bound and destined to be an adventurer for Canada it is we who have the honour and privilege of sitting in this chamber. It is our duty, as such adventurers, to examine with great care everything that is brought before us for consideration, and to shun that which in any way, by any stretch of the imagination, may at any time in the future restrict our freedoms and to retain that which we deem to be good.
I do not believe in excessive verbiage, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe I can be accused of having excessively used the privileges which are mine in this house. I now join the hon. member for Spadina in entering this debate on its fourth or fifth day with the same deep conviction that he expressed in his remarks this afternoon. My convictions may be, and in fact are, somewhat different from his; nevertheless these convictions are born of a consciousness of a responsibility which each and every one of us bears, not only to our own constituents but to the citizens of Canada as a whole.



Defence Production Act
The hon. member for Spadina has had a distinguished career in the service of his fellow Canadians in many spheres. I have had, in a much smaller way, an opportunity to be of service in several different spheres. He and I, in common with many other members in this house, had the misfortune to witness the loss of freedom. We were present together, along with others in Europe, when freedoms were lost. They were lost because of carelessness and lack of interest. We witnessed the hopelessness and the degradation of those who, through their own lack of interest, lost that which is most precious to us and which was then most precious to them. As a result of those experiences the hon. member, in common with myself, is most conscious of our obligations and of our privileges, though I must confess that he puts a slightly different interpretation on those obligations and privileges than I propose to place on them tonight.
We on this side of the house will never attempt to argue that we are any better Canadians than those who sit to your right. Each and every one of us present in this house tonight is conscious of his responsibilities or he or she would not be here. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that some in this house have forgotten something. Some have become careless. But even much of what we do is not important, except that it indicates an attitude of mind. It is that same attitude of mind which resulted in the destruction and desolation which other hon. members and I were permitted to witness not so many years ago.
We require something other than dictation. We require leadership, education and a developed sense of personal discipline. If we need dictation, then I suggest to all members of this house that we in Canada have failed in our pursuit of the freedoms which we all cherish. Let us, therefore, urge development and education, but let us never dictate.
It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, as has been voiced by the minister and by others, that some will fail their country. But I submit that number represents a very small minority, and that the great percentage of Canadians will support everything that is for the good of Canada. Must we therefore dictate to the few and in so doing compel the many?
We have heard the statement that business was not patriotic and would not co-operate. We have heard the statement that some labour unions were not patriotic and would not co-operate. That I do not believe. It is only in isolated instances, as I mentioned before, that we hear of any such case. By the same token we hear about the failure

of modern youth. We hear about hooliganism and about youth running wild. That also I do not believe.
I submit for your consideration, sir, and for the consideration of the house that once again we are hearing about the few isolated instances, not about the many good Canadians who are going about their business in a law-abiding, normal and patriotic way. I have every faith, and I am sure every member in the house has every faith, in the youth of this country. Many members, among whom I was included, were permitted to have the privilege of taking part in what was called an adventure in citizenship. I am sure each and every one present who witnessed any or all of the functions connected with that adventure could come away with only one conclusion; that is, that the future of Canada is in good hands, without dictation.
It strikes me, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that we have forgotten some of the basic tenets of democracy. We must not, as I said before, regiment all for the sake of the few. We must not convict society without a fair trial; and it is in that spirit that I have approached this bill. If I may repeat perhaps ineptly some words of Shakespeare, I would say that I, for my part, come here not to bury Caesar but to plead with him.
My predecessor faced a somewhat similar problem in the house not many years ago. He had the good fortune, or perhaps the misfortune, Mr. Speaker, to sit to your right; and when a certain resolution was debated and voted upon he found he had to stand almost alone in opposition to the granting of powers to the executive which should have been those of the House of Commons.
These powers, Mr. Speaker, were created during an emergency. We were in fact at war. They were created as part of an initial build-up which, in the words of the minister himself, was to last but for a few years. May I quote just one or two remarks of the minister when, in 1951, he said-
There is no particular significance to the date-
He was referring to the expiry date of the act we are asked to amend.
-other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to compare those remarks with those of the minister recently, when he said:
If we get back to a reasonably normal time and the powers are not required I think the government of the day will certainly come forward and revise the act voluntarily.
I ask the obvious question, which has been asked before. What is an emergency, and

what is normal? There we have a difference of opinion. We have a difference of opinion among members of the government themselves. I am not going to quote again the remarks already quoted of the Minister of Defence Production and the Minister of National Defence. Nor am I going to quote or refer to the various shades of opinion expressed in the press and elsewhere, other than to simply reiterate the fact that there is a difference of opinion as to whether or not there is an emergency.
Once again may I come back to what I consider the crux of this argument. That is not whether an emergency exists. The crux of the argument is, shall these admittedly wide powers be made permanent? That, on the one hand, is the contention of the minister. On the other hand, shall these powers in their present form be continued for a defined period, or shall they be continued for an indefinite period in a reduced form?
That is the argument. Let us forget the arguments about whether or not there is an emergency. Let us get down to the basic issue. Are we going to accept these wide powers on an indefinite basis or are we, as we in Her Majesty's loyal opposition contend, going to accept those powers either for a limited period of time or indefinitely on a reduced basis?
One of the reasons advanced by the minister for the extension of the department is stated at page 4501 of Hansard, where he said:
The necessity for extending its life is that it is impossible to hold the class of men we have in the department on the basis of temporary jobs.
It has been said time and again, but it still does not seem to sink in, that we are not advocating the abolition of the department. We are quite prepared to have the department continue-in fact we are enthusiastic about it-but there must be some restriction either on the powers themselves or on their duration.
In developing my next point I should like to place before the house a summary of the act, and in doing so I am not going to attempt to quote from it. I am placing on Hansard for the consideration of yourself, Mr. Speaker, and of hon. members, a summary of some of the powers. I think I am offering a reasonable and a fair summary of powers the minister acquires under the provisions of this act. They are these:
1.	He may compel any industry to accept any contract at a fixed price;
2.	He may requisition any supplies or services or order the production of supplies;
3.	He may fix prices of anything required to carry out the defence program or needed indirectly in connection with the program;
Defence Production Act
4.	He may require any contractor to return any profits which he considers to be excessive, subject to an appeal to the exchequer court;
5.	He may seize the plant of any contractor who he considers is not carrying out a contract efficiently;
6.	He may require anyone who has entered into a contract, voluntarily or otherwise, to make returns of whatever information is needed, and place auditors in any plant at any time; and
7.	He may reduce the amount payable to a contractor at any time during performance of the contract, or afterward.
Having summarized in that brief way the provisions of the act, without elaborating further I should like to ask Your Honour how the provisions of that act, the conveyance of those powers to any one minister, fits into expressions which have been made over the years by a very eminent lawyer, a person who has always been a champion of the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament. The person to whom I refer is, of course, the Prime Minister.
It has been my privilege-and I consider it a privilege-as it has been the privilege of many other hon. members to listen to speeches by the Prime Minister on this very subject. My colleague the hon. member for Greenwood referred to one such speech when he was dealing with the subject of Quebec law. I should like to refer to the presidential address of the Prime Minister to the Canadian Bar Association, which was delivered in October of 1931. He discussed an act known as the unemployment and farm relief act of 1931, and I quote from that speech:
There can be no doubt that our economic system is ill and were it not so. and were not the actual or apprehended gravity of its illness so great. I am sure the former president of this association, the Right Honourable Mr. Bennett, would never have suggested to a British parliament such a departure from ordinary British constitutional practice as is involved in the "act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief, and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada".
The Prime Minister went on to quote the preamble to that act. I consider that the preamble will be of interest to all hon. members on this occasion. It read as follows:
Whereas by reason of the continuing worldwide economic depression there exists in many parts of Canada a serious state of unemployment and distress; and
Whereas the partial failure of the wheat crop of western Canada has intensified the adverse economic conditions theretofore prevailing; and
Whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and other bodies in such

Defence Production Act
ways as the governor in council may deem expedient, and for that purpose should vest in the governor in council the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada;
And so on. Then the Prime Minister quoted sections 2 and 4 of that act. Having done so, he continued his address in the following terms:
A delegation by parliament of its powers in the widest possible terms to the executive authority, for the period during which the act is to remain in force.
May I remind hon. members that perhaps the most significant part of what I am saying now is that section 8 of the act provided that the act was to expire on the 1st day of March, 1932, less than one year from the time it was passed in this house.
The Prime Minister continued:
You will all remember the incisive study of the Canadian situation made just 10 years ago by Viscount Bryce, and which was published under the title of "Canada, An Actual Democracy". He saw us then through very clear eyes, noting many of our qualities and some of our defects, and in estimating the volume and force of public opinion in Canada as compared with European countries, he found that even the large issues were not discussed here on grounds of general principle, but rather on the merits of any particular proposal made.
Further on in his speech, the Prime Minister said:
Perhaps even he-
Referring to Viscount Bryce-
-viewing our economic situation as it exists at the present time and the dangers which it may portend, would feel that we were justified, without ceasing to look upon ourselves as an actual democracy, to indulge in legislation such as that above cited because of its immediate possible benefit, and without fearing that as a deviation from principle it might be setting a dangerous precedent.
I simply emphasize the Prime Minister's remarks at that time by pointing out that we were then in the midst of an emergency no less than we are at the present time; yet the wide powers contained were first of all granted not to the minister but to the governor in council. Second, there was a time limit attached to those powers of something less than one year.

I now desire to refer to some of the remarks made by the minister during his address to this house on June 7. One can come to only one conclusion; one can come only to the conclusion that the Minister of Defence Production does not have the same lofty concept of the law and of the rights of parliament that the Prime Minister of Canada has. I quote from page 4511 of Hansard:

I would draw the attention of hon. members to section 37 which, while it does not permit court action against an investigator or controller in the performance of his duties, goes on to state that "nothing in this section limits or restricts the rights of any person against the crown".

This question was referred to the Department of Justice.

Before the resolution on the present bill was concurred in on March 14, I gave an undertaking that the government would consider the request made by the hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and Peace River (Mr. Low). This request was to include in the act a clause which would make the powers of the department subject to review within a reasonable period.
This request was referred to the Department of Justice, and officers of that department pointed out that in view of the fact that a review of legislation is a matter which parliament can undertake at any time, an express provision requiring a periodic review of this kind would have no real significance. In order to require a review by parliament and attach to it legal consequences it would be necessary, for example, to provide that the act would expire at a stated time unless reviewed and reapproved or re-enacted before the expiration of that time.
Third, I quote from the same page, 4511, in the second column:
There is not the slightest suggestion in the act that personal liberties or freedoms can be menaced or abridged in any way.

Personal liberties are not menaced. The fourth point I should like to refer to in the minister's speech appears at the bottom of page 4511:

Defence Production Act This is the great cure-all; this is the sop that is thrown to us. I ask you to consider this:
This clause gives the person who has been charged an opportunity to establish that he exercised all due diligence to comply with the terms of the act but failed because of reasons beyond his control.
Since when did Magna Carta depart from this parliament? Since when has a man been obliged to prove himself innocent? Since when has the onus of disproof been upon an accused person? Since when has the minister been able to go into court, have his own employees tell their stories, and demand that the accused person not only defend himself but prove that he used due diligence?

In addition, we do not enjoy the leisure and time granted to earlier generations in dealing with threats to peace. When we act we have to act quickly.
