Mr. Speaker, although many members of the house are eager to wind up as soon as possible this session which started January 7 last, it must be obvious that, as long as we members of the official opposition feel it our duty to remain here, we will not hesitate to do so.
If this bill was purposely brought before the house at the tail end of the session, at a time when we are already prostrated by the heat and when fair days beckon us to well deserved relaxation, so that the bill might be railroaded through the house, allow me to say that, between the prospect of recess and our duty of fighting such a dictatorial bill as this one, we did not hesitate and chose to obey the call of duty.

Let me first tell the house that I was greatly surprised to note that the sponsor of this bill is none other than the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He had to identify himself once more with a bill, the enactment of which would have the disastrous consequence of greater and more complete centralization, and be a threat to the supremacy of parliament. No one can convince me that the Prime Minister does not realize the seriousness of his action and does not foresee its nefarious results.
Mr. Speaker, either the Prime Minister of Canada plays a secondary role in the cabinet and must willynilly accept the advice and ambitions of his Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), or he voluntarily agrees to be his confederate in an energetic effort towards greater centralization in Ottawa, thereby once again violating the Canadian constitution.
If, for one as well as the other, such are the purposes they have in mind, they give a rather unworthy example and they shall bequeath to their political friends and successors the memory of a very sad end to a public career. I cannot believe that, at a time when we hear that these two prominent personalities will soon leave the cabinet, they have no more comforting legacy to offer than to have become, before their departure, the unchallenged champions of centralization.
The hon. Minister of Defence Production has vainly tried to make the house and the Canadian people believe that he really needs the powers he is asking for. The only people he has been able to convince are naturally those who, in this house, follow blindly their Liberal masters in every one of their words or deeds, together with the so-called "Liberals in a hurry"-under their true label, the socialists-who rejoice at the prospect that soon a law which they themselves could not have successfully introduced will be included in our statutes.
At a time as tragic as the present, those who have opposed the bill shall be the only ones entitled to call themselves the friends of the people, the faithful upholders of the constitution and the champions of a democracy threatened by a Liberal administration.
If the minister has succeeded in convincing the Prime Minister, the sponsor of this bill, that the dictatorial powers he is asking for

are in his opinion necessary, it means that there exists at the present time in Canada and in the world an alarming situation of an unsuspected seriousness. In this connection, there is something wrong somewhere and some statements must be made to clarify a situation unknown to parliament and to the Canadian people. Nothing in what the Minister of Defence Production has said until now justifies his request.
If we are to believe statements made recently by great statesmen, Sir Anthony Eden, Foster Dulles, the French prime minister and the chancellor of West Germany, it would seem that possible aggressors are at this time most willing to undertake diplomatic negotiations with a view to reducing world tension or the cold war and to establish real peace. Our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), while refusing to be drawn too far, has recently made some rather optimistic statements.
Are the Minister of Defence Production and the Prime Minister the only ones to have a clear insight into world affairs? Are not the great diplomats whose names I have just quoted in a better position than any of us here to tell us what the real situation is?
The powers required would be disquieting enough in a period of open warfare. They are more disquieting still when it is realized that everything points to the possibility of preventing a new world conflict.
If, by the introduction of this bill, the minister and the Prime Minister would have the parliament and the people of this country believe that things will grow much worse in the next few weeks or even in the next few days, they have a duty which they should not shirk, and that is to tell parliament and the people of this country what the true facts of the matter are.
Parliament having been given no indication of the existence of any immediate threat, and convinced as we are that nothing will be officially announced along these lines before the end of this session, I think that we have a right to suspect that the attitude of the Minister of Defence Production and that of the Prime Minister spring from altogether different motives.
Mr. Speaker, like most Canadians and all those who live in countries where the word

It could also be possible to mobilize not only our human resources but all the resources of the country. In a word, the government could control everything.
One might think that I am overdoing it somehow; nevertheless, the way the Liberal party is legislating now, we will be facing all those possibilities.
I remain sceptical, and rightly so, when I hear the sponsors of such legislation tell us that even if they ask for and obtain certain powers, it is not their intention to use them. Nothing could be more nonsensical, because if the legislator does not intend to use a law, why should he take the trouble to draft and discuss it? Why is the government then endeavouring to use its majority to have the bill passed? In other words, to use a comparison, what does a bandit mean to do as he enters a bank, brandishing a pistol, if not to shoot?

The existing Defence Production Act already confers upon the minister powers which are practically limitless, and one has but to read sections 28 and 30 of the said measure to realize how dangerous they are for the future of Canada, of the provinces and of individuals. Here is a paragraph taken from an editorial published in Montreal Matin, on June 14 last:
Sections 28 and 30 by themselves encroach upon our Canadian constitution and upon the rights of the provinces since the first enables the governor in council to annul the obligations which are imposed upon citizens by our provincial laws and since the second empowers the federal government to take control of the entire highway system and of the hydroelectric resources of a province. Ottawa has even the power under section 28 to exempt from any provincial tax any company or corporation entering into a contract with the Department of Defence Production.
Those few sentences found in that Montreal daily prove conclusively I believe that the powers already granted are such as to lead to marked abuse and to dictatorship, purely and simply.
In order to show to the house and to the Canadian people how much what is being done is an insult to the memory of former Liberal leaders, I shall quote various statements made by them, and in so doing show how unworthy of them are those who claim to maintain the same principles.

I was interested to listen to the contribution to the debate by the hon. member for Spadina. I am always interested in his contribution, and certainly some of the statements he made today were rather surprising. He, as well as some other hon. members, referred to the fact that it was difficult just to state when an emergency existed or when it came about. Further on, in reference to that same matter, he mentioned the purpose of this particular bill. He said it would make the bad boys good and keep the good boys good.

Legislation was brought in, or should I say measures were resorted to for that particular purpose, and certainly we in Canada have not had any too much appreciation of the methods that were employed in order to bring about the realization of that objective.
The hon. member for Spadina also suggested that we-I believe he was speaking for the government-should have the power to change their no to yes. He was speaking of industry and those who indicated any hesitation about fitting in with the government's plans and with their defence program. He said they should also have the power to investigate. We see in this measure something we do not like, something we do not think is good for the country. Therefore, because of that fact, we are taking exception to it.
The hon. member for Spadina said the opposition had not got through their minds the important germ of the bill, and stated that it was playing the same record over and over. After listening to the hon. member's speech I can say that it was a replaying of the record we have heard from the government side as well, because he did his best not to bring the matter into the proper perspective. I would suggest that his words and his expressions beclouded the issue and tried to prove that those who were opposing the measure were doing so for reasons other than those we are raising at the present time. Therefore I suggest that possibly he has failed to understand, has failed to grasp the significance of the debate.
I should like to try once again to present and clarify the real reason we in this group are opposed to this particular measure. First of all let me say that we realize the importance and the necessity of this particular department of government. In the debates of the last few days on the defence estimates it has been brought very forcibly to our attention, not only by the words of the Minister of National Defence but by other speakers as well, that dangers continue to confront us in Canada. The world situation is not such as will bring too much comfort or too much optimism. It is true there are indications that some changes have taken place and are taking place, and we certainly hope they are sincere. We sincerely hope that the views, the plans and the objectives of Soviet Russia, for instance, have somehow changed. Nevertheless we do recognize the absolute necessity of a department such as the Department of Defence Production. Not only do we believe it is important that we as a nation keep on our guard, but that we do not succumb in any way to the suggestion that everything has changed and therefore we can reverse our entire defence program.
We are not in line with that idea. We believe we ought to be vigilant; we ought to be on guard. After all, no matter what we gain, if we lose our freedom we lose all. Therefore let me say that this group is in favour of the defence production department. We are not opposing this measure on that score. There are, however, some inherent

dangers in this measure. I believe it can become a fearsome weapon in the hands of an autocratic government or an autocratic minister.
I know many verbal bouquets have been handed the Minister of Defence Production. I realize that, and possibly quite a few of them are deserved. I do not know whether they are all deserved, but anyway we admit a great many of them may be. However, as has been stated on different occasions, we do not know who his successor is going to be.
The other day the Minister of Fisheries referred to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as the minister of fisheries. I do not know whether he had visions of himself occupying the shoes of the Minister of Defence Production a little later on, and had already assigned his particular portfolio to somebody else. I do not know just what was in his mind on that occasion, but I am reminded of a story in old testament history. Solomon, of course, was one of the great kings of days gone by. He was supposed to have been the wisest man who ever lived, but in spite of that fact we are given to understand that his rule and his reign were rather autocratic.
He should have been wise; he had a great many wives.

That is why I sometimes wonder whether he was just as wise as we credit him with being, because he had so many wives. Anyway, the people were labouring under rather severe measures during his reign. Then, after he passed away, Rehoboam came to the throne, and the people sent their representatives to Rehoboam and said: "Your father was a wonderful man, but he was pretty hard on us. The measures under which we were forced to live were rather oppressive, and we would like some relief from those oppressive measures." Rehoboam said, "All right; you come back in about three days' time and I shall give you my answer." So Rehoboam called in the old men who had been his father's counsellors and said, "What do you fellows think about this request? Do you think I ought to accede to their request, lift some of their burdens and ease some of these measures?" They said, "Yes, we think you ought to do it, because if you do it the people will serve you forever."
Not satisfied with that, he called in the young men. He said to them, "What do you suggest?" They said, "Those old fellows, they are all haywire. Don't pay too much attention to them. We would suggest that you add additional burdens, make things heavier; tell them that your little finger is going to be heavier than your father's loins." So when

the people came back to him he heeded that injunction of the young men and placed additional burdens and restrictions on them, and they went away determined that somehow or other they were going to rid themselves of that oppressive ruler.
I tell that story to show that even although the present Minister of Defence Production may be wise and may be only a little autocratic, who is to know what the next man is going to be like? He may place additional restrictions upon us and his authority may be exercised in wider measure until we find that we have a program of regimentation and rigid discipline which none of us in Canada 'want to see brought to pass.
As we look at this measure we realize that it could be used for ulterior purposes. We hope it will be used only for defence purposes, but somehow or other there is a fear that we may be made the victims of a system of regimentation from within against which we are struggling to defend ourselves from without.
In submitting this bill the minister gave some reasons why he did so. He said that in order to have a department adequate to meet the situation they must have all these powers. We are not debating that clause of the bill, because we have no desire to be placed at a disadvantage in time of emergency. We believe the government should be in a position where they can make adequate decisions so we may be prepared for any emergency which may come to pass.
We are not opposing the measure because of the wide powers that are being conferred upon the government or upon the minister. Let me say that one reason we are opposing the measure is the deletion of the expiry clause. The Minister of Defence Production indicated that this would not make any difference as far as the bill was concerned, in view of the statement he made the other day and the amendment he proposed. If the inclusion or exclusion of any expiry date will not make any difference, why is such an adamant stand being taken in respect to it?
I say to the minister, include an expiry date; set it at two, three or four years hence, and I believe you will get the support of this group. But exclude it, and I say we will have no other alternative but to continue to oppose it, and of course when it comes to a vote we shall be forced to vote against it. What has the minister in mind? Is any project contemplated the realization of which requires these absolute powers and an indefinite period of time in order to bring it to fruition? I wonder if there is something like that.
Defence Production Act
I rose tonight to clarify the position of this group and, as I have said before, to state that nothing that has been said in the debate thus far has altered our views or our position. Let me say again that we are not opposing the bill because of the setting up of the department; we are not opposing the bill because of the increasing of the salary; we are not opposing the bill because of the powers that are granted. We are opposing it because there is no expiry date.

Mr. Speaker, in listening to the hon. member for Spadina and the hon. member for Ottawa West today it became fairly obvious that those on the government side of the house believe two things are permanent and will go on forever. Those two things appear to be crises and "C.D." Regardless of how much the Minister of Defence Production has accomplished in this country during the 15 years he has been in Ottawa, regardless of his great abilities and his great failings, the fact is that no minister is a permanent fixture. To argue that broad powers should be granted without a time limit under the Defence Production Act because of the ability, or anything else you want to call it, of the existing minister is to argue upon a basis of fallacy.
May I ask a question? By "C.D." does the hon. member mean civil defence against tyranny?

The hon. member may draw his own conclusion. The other argument that crises are permanent is of course just as invalid as the argument that any single individual is a permanent institution of government.
For the last four years this parliament, by the Defence Production Act, has vested in the present minister what might be called a short-term loan of certain rights and liberties belonging to the people of Canada. By this amendment to remove the time limit from the Defence Production Act the government is asking for a blank cheque by the parliament of Canada and drawn on the account of the people of Canada, payable in the rights and liberties of Canadians now held in that account. The great question is for how many of those rights and liberties would the cheque be filled in by the present or any future minister of defence production. To eliminate the safety factor of the act, the time limit and the right of parliament to review the broad powers vested in one man through this act, is to deprive the people of this country of rights which have been hard fought for and hard won.

I was looking at a book today called "Law and Order in Canadian Democracy" published by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. On page 2 appears a definition of democracy. This is a statement of Gaspard Fauteux, a former Speaker of the House of Commons, who aptly summed it up as follows:
In Canadian democracy the state is the servant of the individual; in other forms of government the individual is the servant of the state.
Then the author of this book goes on to make a comment of his own:
Some totalitarian states call themselves democracies-the country is run for the benefit of its people, but by a small group that holds absolute power; such a "democracy" demands the surrender of all an individual's rights, and the taking over of those rights by the all-powerful state.
Those of us in this group feel strongly that the people of this country have not yet reached the stage where they are willing to hand over to anyone or any group permanent powers that will deprive them of more of their democratic rights. A newspaper in the city of Calgary, my home town, came out with an editorial on Wednesday, June 15, dealing with this particular debate. That editorial is headed "A Fight that is Well Worth Waging". Without quoting directly from the editorial, let me say that it begins with a comment on the House of Commons new air-conditioning system and the fact that the air-conditioning system and time are on the side of the Conservative party, who are, as the newspaper says, putting up a brave and commendable fight against Mr. Howe's attempt to tamper with one of the fundamentals of parliamentary government.

speechtext: The hon. member realizes that he cannot quote from newspapers which comment on proceedings within the house. Abiding by your decision, Mr. Speaker, and without quoting in any way directly from the editorial but paraphrasing what one editor thinks, it might be said that the power the Minister of Defence Production wants, not only for himself but for his successors, regardless of who they might be or to what political party they may belong, is

dangerously far-reaching and as undemocratic as any which has been suggested in any piece of legislation in this or any previous peacetime year.
Order.

The power the minister wants is the right to force any industry in Canada to accept government contracts at what the minister considers the right price, and the power also to seize any industry or industries if they fail to do so. That, of course, is a wartime power and one that has no place whatsoever in a democratic society at any other time than during periods of extreme emergency.
Now, if such a measure as this amendment to the Defence Production Act is ever passed by parliament-and the so-called filibuster staged by the Conservatives and Social Crediters in this house appears to be the only way of opposing it-it will put every industry in this country as well as the individual workers in those industries at the mercy of the government, whether it be the present Liberal government or a future Conservative government.
This editor in Calgary mentions one other point which has not been discussed in the house; and again, without quoting directly from his comments, this is what he suggests. There is another great danger in this amendment eliminating the time factor from this Defence Production Act, and that is the danger that any government could abuse these powers to force industry to contribute to its political campaign funds. During his remarks today the hon. member for Spadina somehow got around to the conclusion that my group in this house were taking the stand they were on this particular bill because we had no hope of ever forming a government in Canada. To that, let me say only this. We have not given up hope by any means of forming a government in Canada.
Two years.

We shall try to hold to the absolute minimum the mess the Conservative government coming up will have to clean up. The hon. member for Ottawa West in his comments today somehow implied that the party of which I am a member was unpatriotic to some degree in trying to apply our amendments to this particular act in a way that would interfere with the legitimate defence needs of this country.
I never said any such thing.

In that regard let me say only
this. Our objective is in no way connected

with any efforts to interfere with the legitimate defence needs of this country, but we do feel we must have safeguards to ensure that any steps taken by the government shall be based upon real grounds of defence needs, and not simply upon grounds which go under the guise of defence. The hon. member for Spadina wound up his remarks with the rather startling conclusion that the purpose of the Conservative party in this so-called filibuster was to try to divide the cabinet and defeat the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Defence Production.
It is already divided.

Mr. Speaker, without attempting to claim any knowledge other than that which comes to all of us through the press of this country who in turn draw much of their information from the usual reliable and informed sources in Ottawa, I think it is fair to say that the cabinet is somewhat divided now on this particular issue. In fact the cabinet seems to be divided on two issues, both introduced by the Minister of Defence Production. The Minister of Defence Production has apparently demanded that the time limit be removed from this act and he will stand for no amendment to it other than the amendment upon which he has now insisted.
There seems to be, according to the press again, some division within the cabinet as to the propriety of permanently granting such powers to any man or any department. The other issue seeming to divide the cabinet in some way concerns this act. I refer, of course, to the division within the cabinet as to the proposal by the Minister of Defence Production for a revision of the government's natural gas pipe-line policy.

As the nation knows, the Minister of Trade and Commerce suffered his first major defeat during his career in Ottawa when he was defeated by members of his own cabinet on the pipe-line issue a few months ago.
